docs.title: FirebirdREST
docs.text:
Serve a RESTful API from any Firebird database.

FirebirdREST is a standalone web server that turns a Firebird database into a REST API, in the spirit of PostgREST. Your tables, views, stored procedures and functions become endpoints, and the grants and roles you already have in Firebird decide what each caller may do. Because the API is derived from the schema, there is no API layer to write or maintain.

$ curl 'http://localhost:3000/books?select=title,price,authors(name)&price=lt.10&order=price.desc'
[
  {"title":"Guards! Guards!","price":9.99,"authors":{"name":"Terry Pratchett"}},
  {"title":"Small Gods","price":8.50,"authors":{"name":"Terry Pratchett"}},
  {"title":"A Wizard of Earthsea","price":7.25,"authors":{"name":"Ursula K. Le Guin"}}
]

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• One static binary for Linux, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD. It talks the Firebird wire protocol directly, so no client library is needed.
  • PostgREST's URL grammar: select, filters, logic trees, ordering and paging.
  • Resource embedding through foreign keys: many-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many, nested, !inner and spread (...rel(cols)).
  • Aggregates: count(), sum(), avg(), min(), max().
  • Computed fields and relationships from functions and procedures.
  • Writes: bulk inserts, upserts, PATCH, PUT and DELETE, returning the written rows on request.
  • Stored procedures and functions, including routines in packages.
  • Security through Firebird roles: a JWT's role claim selects the Firebird ROLE, and claims can be read in PSQL for row-level rules.
  • OpenAPI 3 description at /, CSV output, health endpoints, schema reload on POST_EVENT.
  • Firebird 3, 4 and 5, all tested in CI, plus early testing against the Firebird 6 snapshot.
  • SQL schemas on Firebird 6 (experimental), chosen per request with Accept-Profile and Content-Profile.

docs.text:

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
BinaryDockerGo

Download an archive for your platform from the releases page, for example:

curl -L https://github.com/mariuz/firebirdrest/releases/download/v0.4.0/firebirdrest_0.4.0_linux_amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
./firebirdrest --version

docker run -p 3000:3000 \
  -e FBREST_DB_URI='authenticator:secret@db.example.com:3050/data/app.fdb' \
  -e FBREST_DB_ANON_ROLE=web_anon \
  ghcr.io/mariuz/firebirdrest:latest

go install github.com/mariuz/firebirdrest/cmd/firebirdrest@latest

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: FirebirdREST ships a load tool in bench/ so you can measure it against your own hardware and data.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
# 1. a database with the example schema
isql -user SYSDBA -password masterkey -i examples/bookstore.sql localhost:/data/bench.fdb

# 2. ~400k rows: 2,000 authors, 100,000 books, 200,000 book/tag links,
#    5,000 customers, 50,000 orders with 100,000 items (takes a few seconds)
go run ./bench seed -dsn SYSDBA:masterkey@localhost:3050/data/bench.fdb

# 3. start FirebirdREST against it, then
go run ./bench run -url http://localhost:3000 -c 16 -d 10s -token "$JWT_FOR_WEB_USER"

run prints a Markdown table with requests per second and p50/p95/p99 latency for each scenario. -only <text> runs the matching scenarios only. Scenarios marked "rollback" send Prefer: tx=rollback, so the database is unchanged afterwards.

Measure on a quiet machine

The client, FirebirdREST and Firebird all compete for CPU. With Docker, connect to the container's IP rather than a published port: Docker's userland port proxy cost about 30% of throughput in our runs.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The current code compared with the code before the performance work (commit 712a7fb), on a 4-vCPU Intel Xeon 2.1 GHz VM with 16 GB RAM, Firebird 5.0.4 in Docker on the same machine, 16 concurrent clients, pool of 32 connections. The two versions ran side by side and each scenario alternated between them (median of two 4-second runs) so that drift in the shared VM affects both equally. Absolute numbers depend heavily on hardware; compare the change column.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
Requests that cost about the same in both engines (a row by key, a function call, a 25-row embed) land within 10% of each other: the HTTP and SQL-building layers of the two servers cost about the same, and the rest is the database. The differences come from how each server turns a request into SQL, and from the engines:

  • Embedding with paging (one-to-many, nested, 12–21× faster on FirebirdREST). PostgREST embeds in one statement with a lateral join per level, and PostgreSQL evaluates that join for every parent row the OFFSET skips: at offset=1900 the per-author aggregation runs 1,910 times for 10 result rows (178 ms in EXPLAIN ANALYZE; 560 ms for the three-level nest). FirebirdREST pages the parent rows first and fetches each level's children for those rows only, so the cost doesn't grow with the offset. Page 1 of the same request is fast on both; the advantage is in paging through embedded data, and in to-many embeds of parents with many children.
  • Bulk inserts (100 rows, 11× faster on PostgREST). PostgREST inserts the whole body in one statement (INSERT ... SELECT FROM json_populate_recordset). FirebirdREST used to run one INSERT per row, 100 round trips; since this measurement it sends the rows in EXECUTE BLOCKs (two for this body), which cut a single client's request from 20 ms to 6 ms. Under 16 concurrent clients the gain is only 127 → 191 req/s, because Firebird serializes concurrent inserts into the same table: the time spent in the database grows from 5 ms alone to 75 ms with 16 clients, for the old and the new code alike (a plain PSQL loop inserts 200,000 rows/s on this machine when nothing else writes). That ceiling is the engine's, and the benchmark, with every client inserting into one table, measures it. Single-row inserts are 2× slower than PostgREST's mainly through Firebird's commit cost.
  • Counting and aggregating 100,000 rows (count=exact, group by, 3× faster on PostgREST) and sorting 100,000 rows without an index (filter + order, 2×). These requests scan the whole table on both engines; PostgreSQL scans faster. FirebirdREST's count=planned/estimated avoid the scan when an estimate will do.
  • Pages of 100 rows and computed fields (0.7–0.8× at the time of this table). Counting the wire packets showed why: a read cost 7 round trips to Firebird, of which only two were the query (transaction start, the request context block plus the row-count request the driver added to it, execute, fetch, cursor close, commit). Since this measurement, reads reuse a read-only transaction per connection and the context block runs without the row-count request, which leaves 4 round trips. On the same machine and data, FirebirdREST went from 3,900 to 5,100 req/s on a row by key, 4,200 to 6,600 on the function call, 2,340 to 2,900 on the computed field (parity with PostgREST), 1,800 to 2,460 on the 25-row embed and 1,800 to 2,300 on the 100-row page (0.78× of PostgREST: the rest is the driver's per-row decoding). The next step is in the driver: sending the cursor close together with the following request, as fbclient does, would make it 3.

The absolute numbers are for this machine; the ratios are what to take away. Firebird's engine is generally slower than PostgreSQL's at scanning and aggregating large tables, so an API that does mostly keyed reads, embeds and small writes compares well, and one that counts or groups large tables on every request does not, whichever REST layer is in front.

docs.title: What was optimized
docs.text:
Profiling (admin-pprof = true) showed that time went into database round trips and Firebird compiling statements, not into Go code:

  1. Prepared statement cache. Firebird compiles every statement on prepare, which costs about as much as running a small query. FirebirdREST now keeps up to db-prepared-statements (default 256) compiled statements per role and reuses them across requests. A cache miss runs the query directly and prepares it in the background, so a busy pool can't deadlock.
  2. Request context only when used. Setting the request.* variables was a separate round trip on every request, taking 27% of CPU in the profile. At schema load FirebirdREST checks whether any view, trigger, procedure, function, package or default expression mentions request.. If none does, the step is skipped. When it is needed, all variables (and the db-pre-request procedure) go in one EXECUTE BLOCK.
  3. Faster JSON encoding. Responses are written by an encoder specialised for result rows (no reflection, 2 allocations for a 100-row page) instead of encoding/json, which was 25% of CPU on embed-heavy requests.
  4. Bulk inserts reuse one prepared INSERT for all rows with the same columns.

docs.title: Prepared statements and DDL
docs.text:
Firebird keeps a lock on every table a prepared statement uses. ALTER TABLE and CREATE OR ALTER VIEW work while statements are cached, but DROP TABLE (or dropping a view, procedure, ...) waits until the statements using it are closed. Cached statements unused for db-prepared-statements-idle seconds (default 30) are closed automatically, and a schema reload closes all of them. Before dropping an object that is in active use, reload first:

curl -X POST localhost:3001/reload     # admin server, or: kill -USR1 <pid>

or turn the cache off with db-prepared-statements = 0.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to FirebirdREST are listed here. The project follows semantic versioning; until 1.0, minor versions may change the API.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Reads cost 4 round trips to Firebird instead of 7: GET/HEAD requests reuse a long-lived read-only READ COMMITTED transaction per connection (same results as a fresh one, see Transactions; db-read-tx-reuse = false restores the old behaviour), and the request context block no longer triggers a row-count request. On the benchmark database: a row by key +30%, a function call +60%, a computed field with order +25%, a 25-row embed +30%.
  • Multi-row inserts no longer run one statement per row. On Firebird 4+, a plain insert with return=minimal goes through the wire protocol's batch API (one batch per column set); everything else (Firebird 3, upserts, return=representation, BLOB values) runs in EXECUTE BLOCKs of up to 100 rows that return every row's keys. A 100-row insert takes a third of the time it took, a 1000-row one less. Rows of a view are still inserted one by one. Transactions are now bound to one pooled connection each, which the batch API needs.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Relationships across SQL schemas on Firebird 6: a foreign key between tables of two exposed schemas (db-schemas) is an embeddable relationship in both directions, as in PostgREST, also when the request's schema has a table of the same name. Foreign keys into schemas that aren't exposed stay out (schemas).
  • Benchmarks against PostgREST on identical data, with the PostgreSQL schema and seed in bench/postgrest/ and the results and their interpretation on the Benchmarks page.
  • A stability promise saying which interfaces are stable, which are experimental, and how deprecations and behaviour changes are announced, and an upgrade guide with the changes to check for each version.
  • firebirdrest -check [config-file] validates the configuration and prints warnings without connecting; the warnings are also logged at startup. Deprecated setting names, when there are any, keep working for a minor version with a warning.

Production readiness: Prometheus metrics, Server-Timing, JWKS keys from identity providers with a token cache, single values and files in any media type, raw bodies for RPC, and the fixes of a security review. A JavaScript client with the supabase-js API, firebirdrest-js, checks compatibility in CI.

Behaviour changes to check before upgrading:

  • server-cors-allowed-origins = "*" no longer sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials; list the origins explicitly if browsers must send credentials.
  • GET / describes only what the caller's role is granted; set openapi-mode = "ignore-privileges" for the old document.
  • Requests are limited to 60 seconds and 16 MB bodies (server-request-timeout, server-max-body-size), and and=/or= nesting to 16 levels, in.() to 1000 values.
  • Permission errors no longer include Firebird's "Effective user is ..." line, and unexpected errors return a generic message (the cause is logged).
  • Pool and statement cache metrics label roles in upper case.
  • Responses carry X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and a sandboxing Content-Security-Policy.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
A review of the SQL generation, authentication and HTTP surface found no injection or authentication bypass, and these weaknesses, all fixed here:

  • A deeply nested and=/or= filter or a long in.() list could take the Firebird connection down or burn CPU for tens of seconds: nesting is limited to 16 levels and in.() to 1000 values (400 beyond).
  • A Range header with a huge end overflowed the limit arithmetic and removed db-max-rows; such ranges are refused with 416.
  • A single value requested as text/html (or SVG, XML, script) was served as a page of the API's origin: stored script in a column could run there. Every response now carries X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and a sandboxing Content-Security-Policy, and those types are sent as downloads.
  • With the default server-cors-allowed-origins = "*", any origin was reflected together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; the wildcard now answers * without credentials, and only listed origins get credentials (with Vary: Origin).
  • GET / described every table and routine to anonymous callers. The document now follows the caller's privileges (openapi-mode, default follow-privileges).
  • Permission errors named the database login ("Effective user is ..."), and unexpected errors returned their internal text; both are now generic for the client and logged on the server.
  • Each case spelling of a role name (web_user, WEB_USER...) opened its own connection pool; names are folded to upper case, as Firebird does.
  • The HTTP server had no request timeout and read request bodies inside the transaction: server-request-timeout (60 s), server-max-body-size (16 MB) and header limits are enforced, and bodies are read before the transaction starts.
  • An empty boolean in the config file (admin-pprof =) counted as true; it now keeps the default.
  • admin-server-host binds the admin server to its own address, e.g. 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Metrics in the Prometheus format at GET /metrics on the admin port: requests by method and status, a request duration histogram, error codes, connection pool and statement cache usage per role, schema cache loads, JWT cache and JWKS fetches, and Go runtime figures. See Monitoring.
  • server-timing-enabled adds a Server-Timing header (jwt, parse, transaction, response), as in PostgREST.
  • jwt-secret accepts a JWK or a JWKS as JSON, PEM certificates and PKCS#1 RSA keys, several PEM keys at once, Ed25519 keys (EdDSA) and @/path/to/file; PS256/384/512 tokens are accepted with RSA keys. Tokens with a kid are checked against the matching key.
  • jwt-secret-is-base64 for base64 encoded HMAC secrets.
  • jwt-jwks-url fetches the signing keys of an identity provider (Auth0, Keycloak, Okta, Azure AD, ...) at startup and every jwt-jwks-refresh seconds, and again when a token names an unknown kid, so rotated keys work right away.

  • A JWT validation cache (jwt-cache-max-entries, default 1000) skips the signature check for tokens already accepted, until they expire or for 5 minutes.

  • Single values as is: any concrete Accept type that isn't a built-in format (text/plain, application/octet-stream, image/png, application/geo+json...) returns the one selected value of the one matching row as the body, with that Content-Type. Binary columns are sent as their bytes, so files can be served straight from the database. Works for reads, writes with return=representation and RPC.

  • Raw request bodies for RPC: a POST /rpc/<name> whose Content-Type isn't JSON or a form puts the body into the routine's only parameter, as text or bytes (FBRST133 otherwise).
  • The example database has a covers table with a binary BLOB and a blob_size function.
  • A raw single-value response sends a binary value as the driver returns it, without a base64 encode/decode round trip, so serving a file holds one copy of it in memory.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Accept entries with a parameter that has no value, such as the application/vnd.pgrst.plan+text; for="application/json"; options=; that postgrest-js sends for explain(), were rejected with 406. The media type is now read even when a parameter is malformed.

  • Responses are sent only after the transaction commits. A failed COMMIT now returns an error instead of a success response, and headers set before an error (such as Content-Range on a 416) no longer appear on the error response.

  • Graceful shutdown waits for requests in flight (up to 10 seconds) before closing the database connections; before, requests running at SIGTERM could fail with 500.

SQL schemas for Firebird 6, chosen per request with Accept-Profile and Content-Profile. Schema support is experimental: it is tested against the Firebird 6 snapshot and may change if Firebird 6 changes before its release. Existing setups keep working as before: Firebird 3-5 are unaffected, and Firebird 6 without db-schemas serves PUBLIC as it did.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • SQL schemas (Firebird 6, experimental): db-schemas lists the schemas to expose, the first being the default (public when unset). Requests pick one with Accept-Profile (reads) or Content-Profile (writes), as in PostgREST; responses carry Content-Profile, and unexposed schemas get 406 (FBRST106). Each schema has its own cache and OpenAPI description, statements use schema-qualified names, and embedding follows foreign keys within the schema. examples/bookstore-fb6.sql adds an inventory schema. db-pre-request accepts schema.proc.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • On Firebird 6 the schema cache matches system-table rows by schema as well as by name (domains, constraints, indexes, routine parameters), instead of relying on names being unique.
Write guards with max-affected, query plans, and per-request time zones.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Prefer: handling=strict refuses unknown or invalid preferences (FBRST130); the default lenient ignores them, as before.
  • Prefer: max-affected=n (with handling=strict, as in PostgREST): a PATCH or DELETE that would change more than n rows fails with FBRST131 and is rolled back.
  • Query plans: with db-plan-enabled = true, Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.plan (+text or +json) returns Firebird's explained plan of every statement a GET/HEAD request runs, including embeds and counts, instead of the data.
  • Prefer: timezone=<IANA name> (Firebird 4+): TIME/TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE values are returned in that zone, and the Firebird session runs in it (SET TIME ZONE, reset before the connection is reused). Unknown zones are ignored, or refused with handling=strict.
  • examples/bookstore-fb4.sql adds a meetings table with time zone columns for Firebird 4+.
  • The release workflow can also publish the Docker image to Docker Hub, a Homebrew cask and a Scoop manifest, each once its secret is configured (see RELEASING.md).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Release notes are taken from the version's section of CHANGELOG.md, also for a release first drafted on GitHub. RELEASING.md describes the release steps.
Ordering by embedded columns, limited PATCH/DELETE, bulk RPC calls, estimated counts, and Firebird 6 support (tested against the 6.0 snapshot).

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Ordering by a column of a to-one embed, as in PostgREST: order=authors(name).desc. It works at any level (books.order=authors(name)), by alias and on spread embeds. To-many embeds are refused with FBRST126.
  • PATCH and DELETE with limit and offset, as in PostgREST: ?order=created_at&limit=10 changes only the first 10 matching rows. A limit needs an order (FBRST127), and the primary key is added to it as a tie-breaker. db-safe-updates accepts a limit instead of a filter.
  • Prefer: params=multiple-objects on /rpc: an array body calls the routine once per object in one transaction. Selectable procedures return the combined rows as one result (one UNION ALL query, so select, filters, order and limit apply to all of them; at most 200 objects), executable procedures and functions an array of results.
  • Prefer: params=single-object on /rpc: the raw JSON body is passed to a routine's only text parameter. The example database has log_request for this.
  • Prefer: count=planned and count=estimated. planned estimates a table's rows from the statistics of its unique indexes without reading the table; estimated counts exactly up to db-max-rows (or 1000) and uses the estimate above. Where no estimate applies (filters, views, procedures, no statistics) the count is exact and Preference-Applied says count=exact. Unknown count= values are ignored instead of being treated as exact. The example database computes its index statistics after loading data.
  • CI runs the integration suite against the Firebird 6 snapshot (firebirdsql/firebird:6-snapshot) on every push and weekly. The job may fail without failing the build until Firebird 6 is released.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A PATCH with ?limit= and return=representation updated every matching row but returned only limit of them; the limit now applies to the update itself.
  • Schema loading reports errors that happen while reading the system tables, instead of silently loading an incomplete schema (on Firebird 6 this hid every foreign key).
  • Foreign keys and unique constraints load on Firebird 6.
  • On Firebird 6, the hint of a PSQL exception names the exception without the "PUBLIC". schema prefix, as on earlier versions.
First release. Supports Firebird 3, 4 and 5.

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
• Tables and views at /<name>, with PostgREST's URL grammar: select (aliases, casts), filters (eq, neq, gt, gte, lt, lte, like, ilike, in, is, isdistinct, not.), plus Firebird's containing, starting and similar; nested or/and trees; order; limit/offset and the Range header; Prefer: count=exact.
  • Resource embedding through foreign keys: many-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many through junction tables, nested embeds, !hint disambiguation, !inner, embed=is.null, and per-embed filters, order and limits.
  • Spread embeds (...rel(cols)): to-one values are merged into the parent; to-many columns become arrays.
  • Aggregates count(), sum(), avg(), min(), max() with automatic grouping, inside embeds too (authors?select=name,books(count)).
  • Computed fields (PSQL functions) and computed relationships (selectable and executable procedures) declared with TYPE OF COLUMN parameters.
  • JSON, CSV and single-object (application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) responses.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
• POST (single or bulk), upserts with Prefer: resolution=merge-duplicates|ignore-duplicates and on_conflict, PATCH, PUT, DELETE, Prefer: return=representation with select and embeds, ?columns=, Prefer: missing=default, Prefer: tx=rollback.
  • PATCH/DELETE without filters are refused unless db-safe-updates = false.

docs.title: Routines
docs.text:
• /rpc/<name> for selectable procedures (filterable like tables), executable procedures and PSQL functions, plus public routines of packages at /rpc/<package>.<name>.
  • GET requests run in read-only transactions.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• Prepared statement cache per role (db-prepared-statements, default 256), with idle expiry (db-prepared-statements-idle, default 30 s) so DROP statements are not blocked.
  • The request.* context variables are only set when the database reads them (db-request-context = auto|always|never), in a single EXECUTE BLOCK together with db-pre-request.
  • Faster JSON encoding of result rows; bulk inserts reuse one prepared statement.
  • See docs/benchmarks.md for numbers and the load tool.

docs.title: Security and operations
docs.text:
• JWT (HS256/384/512 secret, or RS/ES public key) mapped to Firebird roles; anonymous role; requests are refused if the role isn't granted to the database user.
  • JWT claims, role, method, path and selected headers exposed to PSQL through RDB$GET_CONTEXT('USER_TRANSACTION', ...); optional db-pre-request procedure.
  • OpenAPI 3 document at /.
  • Schema cache reload with POST_EVENT 'fbrest_reload', SIGUSR1 or POST /reload on the admin server, which also serves /live and /ready.
  • Config file or FBREST_* environment variables; CORS; Docker image and docker-compose example.
  • Documentation site at https://mariuz.github.io/firebirdrest/ (built from docs/).
  • bench/ load tool with a data seeder.
  • admin-pprof serves Go profiling endpoints on the admin port.
  • Release workflow can be started from GitHub (Actions, then Release, then Run workflow).

docs.title: Differences from PostgREST
docs.text:
FirebirdREST borrows PostgREST's URL grammar, Prefer headers, error shape and security model, so PostgREST client libraries and habits mostly carry over. Firebird is not PostgreSQL, though.

firebirdrest-js wraps supabase-js's query builder (@supabase/postgrest-js) for FirebirdREST; its test suite is the compatibility check for the list below.

docs.title: Same
docs.text:
• select with aliases, casts, embedding, !hint, !inner, spread (...) and aggregates.
  • Filters eq, neq, gt, gte, lt, lte, like, ilike, in, is, isdistinct, not., and or/and trees.
  • order (including order=embed(column) on to-one embeds), limit, offset, Range, Prefer: count=exact, count=planned and count=estimated.
  • POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE (PATCH/DELETE with order and limit), Prefer: return=…, resolution=…, missing=default, tx=rollback, on_conflict, columns.
  • /rpc/<name> with GET (read-only) and POST, Prefer: params=multiple-objects and params=single-object.
  • JWT role switching, an anonymous role, a pre-request hook, and claims available to SQL.
  • jwt-secret as an HMAC secret (also base64 encoded), a PEM key, a JWK or a JWKS, or @file; a JWT validation cache.
  • server-timing-enabled and the Server-Timing header (jwt, parse, transaction, response).
  • application/vnd.pgrst.object+json, CSV, OpenAPI at /, {code, message, details, hint} errors.
  • Prefer: handling=strict, max-affected and timezone; query plans with Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.plan (behind db-plan-enabled).

docs.title: Different
docs.text:
Topic PostgREST FirebirdREST Namespaces exposed schemas, Accept-Profile the same on Firebird 6 (db-schemas, Accept-Profile, Content-Profile); Firebird 3–5 have no schemas: one namespace. Packaged routines are /rpc/package.name Relationships across schemas foreign keys into other exposed schemas the same on Firebird 6: foreign keys between exposed schemas embed both ways Identifier case as stored unquoted (upper case) names shown in lower case Claims in SQL current_setting('request.jwt.claims')::json RDB$GET_CONTEXT('USER_TRANSACTION', 'request.jwt.claim.<name>'), one variable per claim (Firebird has no JSON functions) Computed fields / relationships functions taking a table row routines whose parameters are TYPE OF COLUMN <table>.<col> To-one computed relationship function returning one row executable procedure Extra operators fts, cs, cd, ov, JSON ->/->>, ranges, arrays Firebird's containing, starting, similar; no JSON, array or range types in Firebird Aggregates off by default on by default (db-aggregates-enabled) Embedding one SQL statement with lateral joins one batched query per embed level Roles SET ROLE per transaction a connection pool per role (Firebird sets the role at connect time) Metrics pgrst_* metrics on the admin server firebirdrest_* metrics with their own names, at /metrics on the admin port (list) JWT keys from a URL not built in jwt-jwks-url fetches a provider's JWKS and follows key rotation JWT cache size jwt-cache-max-entries the same; entries also expire after 5 minutes and when the JWKS changes Schema reload NOTIFY pgrst POST_EVENT 'fbrest_reload' Unfiltered PATCH/DELETE allowed (unless pg-safeupdate) refused unless db-safe-updates = false Request context cost always set only when the database reads it (db-request-context) params=single-object the body goes to a single json parameter the body goes to a single text parameter, as JSON text params=multiple-objects on set-returning routines no limit at most 200 objects per request count=planned the planner's estimate of the query the table's row count from index statistics; exact for filtered requests, views and procedures Query plans EXPLAIN output (text or JSON), also for writes Firebird's explained plan per statement, for GET/HEAD only Prefer: timezone changes how timestamptz is displayed WITH TIME ZONE values carry a zone in Firebird, so they are converted to the requested zone; ignored on Firebird 3

| Custom media types | handler functions per media type | any concrete Accept type returns a single value as is (details); a raw request body goes to a routine's only parameter | | application/geo+json | built in | request it from a function that returns GeoJSON text |

Open an issue if you miss something.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: FirebirdREST keeps no state outside its configuration and the database, so an upgrade is a new binary or image and a restart. What needs attention is listed per version below; the stability promise says what never changes without notice.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Read the changelog entries between your version and the new one, starting with each version's behaviour changes to check before upgrading.
  2. Check the configuration with the new binary before rolling it out: 
    firebirdrest -check /etc/firebirdrest.conf
    It loads the configuration (file and FBREST_* variables), reports unknown or invalid settings and deprecation warnings, and exits with status 0 when all is well. Nothing is connected or served.
  3. Deploy. With several instances behind a load balancer, roll them one at a time; the admin endpoint GET /ready returns 200 once an instance has loaded its schema cache.
  4. If something is wrong, roll back to the previous binary or image tag: nothing in the database or the configuration format changes between versions.

Client code written against the documented API keeps working. If you use firebirdrest-js, its suite skips features newer than the server, so a newer client works with an older server.

docs.title: 0.3.0 → 0.4.0
docs.text:
Three behaviour changes, from the performance work and the schema support:

Change Who is affected What to do GET/HEAD requests reuse a read-only READ COMMITTED transaction per connection instead of starting one each; a transaction serves up to 1000 requests or 5 minutes. Results are the same as with a fresh transaction. Monitoring that counts transactions on the Firebird side; a db-pre-request procedure that relies on transaction-level state between requests. Nothing for most deployments. db-read-tx-reuse = false restores one transaction per request. Multi-row inserts run as one batch (Firebird 4+, return=minimal) or in EXECUTE BLOCKs of up to 100 rows, and a transaction is bound to one pooled connection. Triggers or procedures that observe how rows arrive, e.g. counting statements; db-pool = 1 deployments, where a read transaction and a write now take turns on the single connection. Nothing for most deployments. Rows of a view are still inserted one by one. On Firebird 6, a foreign key between tables of two exposed schemas is an embeddable relationship. Clients that relied on such an embed being refused with FBRST200. Nothing; expose only the schemas that may be embedded.

New: firebirdrest -check, the benchmarks page and the stability promise change no behaviour.

docs.title: 0.2.x → 0.3.0
docs.text:
Six behaviour changes, all from the security review and the monitoring work:

Change Who is affected What to do The CORS wildcard (server-cors-allowed-origins = "*", the default) answers Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and no longer sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Browser clients that send cookies or HTTP auth from a proxy in front of FirebirdREST. Bearer tokens set by JavaScript are not affected. List the origins explicitly: server-cors-allowed-origins = "https://app.example". GET / describes only what the caller's role is granted (openapi-mode = "follow-privileges"). Tools that fetched the whole schema anonymously, e.g. a code generator run without a token. Send a token with the role whose view you want, or set openapi-mode = "ignore-privileges". Requests are limited: 60 s (server-request-timeout), 16 MB bodies (server-max-body-size), and=/or= nested at most 16 levels, at most 1000 values in in.(). Bulk inserts over 16 MB, uploads, long-running procedures, generated filters with huge in lists. Raise server-max-body-size or server-request-timeout (0 disables the timeout); split long in lists over requests or use a selectable procedure. Permission errors no longer include Firebird's "Effective user is ..." line; unexpected errors return internal server error and the cause goes to the log. Anything matching on those strings. Match on code (SQLSTATE 28000, FBRST000) instead. Pool and statement cache metrics label roles in upper case (role="WEB_USER"). Prometheus queries and dashboards. Update the label values. Every response carries X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox; single values requested as HTML, SVG, XML, script or PDF are sent as downloads. Pages that embedded API URLs directly as documents. Serve such content through your application, or request it with fetch and render it there.

New settings have defaults that keep the old behaviour otherwise: jwt-secret-is-base64, jwt-jwks-url, jwt-jwks-refresh, jwt-cache-max-entries, server-timing-enabled, admin-server-host.

docs.title: 0.1.x → 0.2.0
docs.text: No behaviour changes. db-schemas is new and off by default; on Firebird 6 the PUBLIC schema is served as before.

docs.title: 0.1.0 → 0.1.1 and 0.1.2
docs.text: No behaviour changes. New preferences (count=planned, count=estimated, handling=strict, max-affected, timezone, params=...) are off unless sent; query plans need db-plan-enabled.

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
select accepts count(), sum(), avg(), min() and max(). Every other selected column becomes part of the GROUP BY.

GET /books?select=count()
[{"count":5}]

GET /books?select=author_id,count(),total:price.sum(),price.avg()&order=author_id
[{"author_id":1,"count":2,"total":18.49,"avg":9.24}, ...]

GET /books?select=in_stock,count()&order=in_stock
[{"in_stock":false,"count":1},{"in_stock":true,"count":4}]

GET /books?select=published.min(),published.max()
[{"min":1961,"max":1992}]
  • The key is the function name unless you give an alias (total:price.sum()).
  • count() counts rows; column.count() counts non-null values.
  • Casts apply to the result: price.sum()::text.
  • Filters apply before grouping (SQL WHERE).
  • order may use the grouped columns.
  • Prefer: count=exact counts the groups.

Firebird's typing applies: avg() of an integer column returns an integer (1976.8 becomes 1976). Cast the column to numeric or double in a view, or use a computed field, if you need the fraction.

docs.title: Inside embeds
docs.text:
Aggregates in an embed are computed per parent row:

GET /authors?select=name,books(count)
[{"name":"Terry Pratchett","books":[{"count":2}]}, ...]

GET /authors?select=name,books(count(),price.sum())

Inside an embed, plain count is short for count(). A parent without related rows gets [{"count":0}]. Spread the embed to get flat values:

GET /authors?select=name,...books(count(),total:price.sum())
[{"name":"Terry Pratchett","count":2,"total":18.49}, ...]

docs.title: Turning them off
docs.text: Aggregates over large tables can be expensive. Set db-aggregates-enabled = false to reject them with 400.

docs.title: Computed fields and relationships
docs.text:
A function or procedure whose input parameters are all declared TYPE OF COLUMN <table>.<column> of the same table is attached to that table. FirebirdREST passes the row's columns as arguments. You don't need to configure anything else.

Routine Becomes Example PSQL function a computed field books?select=title,price_with_vat Selectable procedure (with SUSPEND) a to-many relationship (array) books?select=title,similar_books(title) Executable procedure a to-one relationship (object of its output parameters) authors?select=name,author_stats(*)

PostgREST does this with functions that take a table row as their argument. Firebird routines can't, so the TYPE OF COLUMN declaration marks which table a routine belongs to.

docs.title: Computed fields
docs.text:
CREATE FUNCTION price_with_vat (price TYPE OF COLUMN books.price)
RETURNS NUMERIC(12,2)
AS
BEGIN
  RETURN price * 1.19;
END

CREATE FUNCTION label (title TYPE OF COLUMN books.title, published TYPE OF COLUMN books.published)
RETURNS VARCHAR(220)
AS
BEGIN
  RETURN title || ' (' || published || ')';
END

A computed field works like a column in select, filters, order and aggregates:

GET /books?select=id,label,price_with_vat&price_with_vat=gt.12&order=price_with_vat.desc
[{"id":3,"label":"The Dispossessed (1974)","price_with_vat":14.28},{"id":5,"label":"Solaris (1961)","price_with_vat":12.38}]

GET /books?select=price_with_vat.sum()

Computed fields are not included in select=*; name them.

docs.title: To-many relationships
docs.text:
CREATE PROCEDURE similar_books (book_id TYPE OF COLUMN books.id, author_id TYPE OF COLUMN books.author_id)
RETURNS (id INTEGER, title VARCHAR(200))
AS
BEGIN
  FOR SELECT b.id, b.title FROM books b
      WHERE b.author_id = :author_id AND b.id <> :book_id
      INTO :id, :title
  DO SUSPEND;
END

GET /books?select=title,similar_books(title)
GET /books?select=title,similar_books(title)&similar_books.title=starting.S&similar_books.limit=3
GET /books?select=title,similar_books!inner(title)       # only books that have similar ones
GET /books?select=title,similar_books(count)
GET /books?select=title,...similar_books(similar:title)  # spread: "similar":["Small Gods"]

The procedure runs once per distinct parent key, all in one batched query:

SELECT ... FROM (SELECT DISTINCT k.ID, k.AUTHOR_ID FROM BOOKS k WHERE k.ID IN (...)) k
CROSS JOIN SIMILAR_BOOKS(k.ID, k.AUTHOR_ID) t0

docs.title: To-one relationships
docs.text:
CREATE PROCEDURE author_stats (author_id TYPE OF COLUMN authors.id)
RETURNS (book_count INTEGER, avg_price NUMERIC(10,2))
AS
BEGIN
  SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(b.price) FROM books b WHERE b.author_id = :author_id
    INTO :book_count, :avg_price;
END

GET /authors?select=name,author_stats(*)
[{"name":"Terry Pratchett","author_stats":{"book_count":2,"avg_price":9.24}}, ...]

GET /authors?select=name,stats:author_stats(n:book_count)
GET /authors?select=name,...author_stats(book_count)

An executable procedure runs once per distinct parent key with EXECUTE PROCEDURE. Firebird can't select from it, so filters, order, paging, aggregates and !inner are not available on to-one computed relationships. Use a selectable procedure if you need them.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The request's role needs EXECUTE on the routine, and the routine needs access to the tables it reads:

GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION price_with_vat TO ROLE web_anon;
GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE similar_books TO ROLE web_anon;
GRANT SELECT ON books TO PROCEDURE similar_books;

docs.title: Resource embedding
docs.text: Foreign keys connect tables. Name a related table in select, with its own column list in parentheses, and its rows are nested into the response.

docs.title: Relationship kinds
docs.text:
GET /books?select=title,authors(name)              # many-to-one: an object (or null)
GET /authors?select=name,books(title,price)        # one-to-many: an array
GET /books?select=title,tags(name)                 # many-to-many: an array

[{"title":"Guards! Guards!","authors":{"name":"Terry Pratchett"}}]
[{"name":"Terry Pratchett","books":[{"title":"Guards! Guards!","price":9.99},{"title":"Small Gods","price":8.50}]}]
[{"title":"Guards! Guards!","tags":[{"name":"fantasy"},{"name":"humour"}]}]

Many-to-many relationships go through a junction table whose primary key consists of foreign keys to both sides, like book_tags (book_id, tag_id). A one-to-many relationship whose foreign key is also the child's primary key is treated as one-to-one and returns an object.

Embeds nest to any depth:

GET /customers?select=email,orders(status,order_items(qty,books(title,authors(name))))

docs.title: Naming and disambiguation
docs.text:
GET /books?select=title,writer:authors(name)        # alias the key
GET /books?select=title,author_id(name)             # embed by the foreign key column

When two foreign keys connect the same tables, FirebirdREST answers 300 Multiple Choices and lists them. Pick one with ! followed by the constraint name or the column:

GET /orders?select=*,customers!fk_orders_customer(name)
GET /orders?select=*,billing:customers!billing_customer_id(name),shipping:customers!shipping_customer_id(name)

docs.title: Filtering, ordering and limiting embeds
docs.text:
Prefix a parameter with the embed's name (or alias) to apply it to the embedded rows:

GET /authors?select=name,books(title,price)&books.price=gt.9&books.order=price.desc&books.limit=1
GET /authors?select=name,books(title)&books.or=(title.ilike.*sea*,title.ilike.*star*)
GET /customers?select=email,orders(order_items(qty))&orders.order_items.qty=gt.1

These filters only remove embedded rows. Parents are always returned, with an empty array or null when nothing matches, like a LEFT JOIN.

docs.title: Filtering parents by their embeds
docs.text:
!inner keeps only the parents that have at least one matching embedded row:

GET /books?select=title,authors!inner(name)&authors.country=eq.Poland
GET /books?select=title,tags!inner(name)&tags.name=eq.humour

<embed>=is.null and <embed>=not.is.null keep the parents without, or with, related rows:

GET /books?select=title,tags(name)&tags=is.null        # books without tags
GET /authors?select=name,books(title)&books=not.is.null

These turn into EXISTS (...) conditions on the parent query, so they also work with limit, order and Prefer: count=exact.

docs.title: Spread
docs.text:
... merges an embed's columns into the parent instead of nesting them.

To-one (many-to-one, one-to-one, executable computed relationships): the values themselves.

GET /books?select=title,...authors(author:name,country)

[{"title":"Guards! Guards!","author":"Terry Pratchett","country":"UK"}]

To-many (one-to-many, many-to-many, selectable computed relationships): one array per column, in the embed's order.

GET /authors?select=name,...books(title,price)&books.order=price.desc
GET /books?select=title,...tags(tag:name)

[{"name":"Terry Pratchett","title":["Guards! Guards!","Small Gods"],"price":[9.99,8.50]}]
[{"title":"Guards! Guards!","tag":["fantasy","humour"]}]

A spread of aggregates only gives plain values, because there is one row per parent:

GET /authors?select=name,...books(count(),total:price.sum())

[{"name":"Terry Pratchett","count":2,"total":18.49}]

Spread embeds can't have an alias. If a spread column would collide with another key (both tables have a name), the request fails with a hint; rename one with an alias, as in ...tags(tag:name).

docs.title: Key order
docs.text: Keys appear in the order of select, embeds included: select=authors(name),title puts authors first.

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text: Each embed level is one extra query, batched for all parents with IN (...). select=a,b(c(d)) over 25 rows makes three queries, not 1 + 25 + 25×n. Per-parent limit/offset on embeds are applied after fetching, so books.limit=1 still reads every book of the authors on the page.

docs.title: Response formats
docs.text:
Choose with the Accept header:

Accept Response application/json (default, also */*) JSON array of objects text/csv header row plus one line per row; embedded values are written as JSON application/vnd.pgrst.object+json a single JSON object, or 406 unless exactly one row matches any other concrete type, e.g. text/plain, application/octet-stream, image/png a single value as is: see below 
curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=id,title' -H 'Accept: text/csv'
curl 'localhost:3000/books?id=eq.1' -H 'Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json'

docs.title: Single values and files
docs.text:
Ask for any concrete media type that isn't in the table above, and the response body is the value itself instead of JSON, with the Content-Type you asked for. The request must select one column and match one row:

# the bytes of a BLOB SUB_TYPE BINARY column, served as an image
curl 'localhost:3000/covers?select=image&book_id=eq.1' -H 'Accept: image/png' > cover.png
# a text column, as text
curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=summary&id=eq.1' -H 'Accept: text/plain'
# a function result, as text
curl 'localhost:3000/rpc/add_vat?amount=100' -H 'Accept: text/plain'
  • Binary columns (BLOB SUB_TYPE BINARY, CHARACTER SET OCTETS) are sent as their bytes; text columns as their text; numbers, booleans and dates as their JSON text (9.99, true). text/*, +json and +xml types get ; charset=utf-8.
  • NULL gives an empty 204.
  • Types a browser would run or render as a document (text/html, SVG, XML, JavaScript, PDF) are sent as downloads (Content-Disposition: attachment), so a stored value can never run as a page of the API.
  • More than one row gives 406 (FBRST116), more than one column 406 (FBRST107).
  • application/octet-stream works for any column. A column's own type (image/png, application/pdf) is handy to serve files straight from the database; keep the type in another column if it varies per row, and read it first.
  • This also covers formats FirebirdREST doesn't produce itself: a function that builds GeoJSON text can be requested with Accept: application/geo+json.
  • It works for /rpc functions, procedures with one output parameter, selectable procedures, and writes with Prefer: return=representation (for example POST /covers?select=book_id).
  • A built-in type anywhere in Accept, or a wildcard, takes precedence: a browser's text/html, */* still gets JSON.

docs.title: Binary data and memory
docs.text:
In JSON, BLOB SUB_TYPE BINARY and CHARACTER SET OCTETS values are base64 strings, and are sent the same way on input. Firebird returns a BLOB as a whole, so each BLOB in a response is held in memory while the request runs: a raw single-value response holds it once, a JSON response also holds its base64 form. Keep that in mind for large files:

  • Select only the columns you need: select=* includes BLOB columns.
  • Serve files with a raw single-value request (above) rather than through JSON.
  • To show sizes without reading the data, expose OCTET_LENGTH(image) through a computed field.
  • db-max-rows bounds the number of rows, not their size.

docs.title: Query plans
docs.text:
To see how Firebird runs a request, ask for its plan instead of its data. This is off by default, because plans show table and index names: set db-plan-enabled = true (for example in development).

curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=title,authors(name)&price=lt.10' -H 'Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.plan'

-- statement 1
SELECT t0."TITLE", t0."AUTHOR_ID" FROM "BOOKS" t0 WHERE ((t0."PRICE" < ?))

Select Expression
    -> Filter
        -> Table "BOOKS" as "T0" Full Scan

-- statement 2
SELECT t0."NAME", t0."ID" FROM "AUTHORS" t0 WHERE (t0."ID" IN (?, ?))

Select Expression
    -> Filter
        -> Table "AUTHORS" as "T0" Access By ID
            -> Bitmap
                -> Index "RDB$PRIMARY1" List Scan (full match)

Here price has no index, so the books are read with a full scan.

  • The response lists every statement the request runs: one per embed level, and the count with Prefer: count=exact. The plan is Firebird's explained plan (MON$EXPLAINED_PLAN).
  • application/vnd.pgrst.plan+json returns [{"query": "...", "plan": "..."}]; application/vnd.pgrst.plan and +text return text.
  • Plans are available for GET and HEAD (reads and selectable procedures). To know the statements of embedded resources the request is run in its read-only transaction, with the result discarded. Other methods are refused with 405 (FBRST132): they would have to write.
  • With plans disabled, the plan media types get 406.

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
GET / returns an OpenAPI 3 document describing the tables, views, procedures and functions the caller's role may use, with their columns, types, keys and computed fields, and only the methods the role is granted (SELECT → get, INSERT → post, ...). Send the request with the token whose view you want; without one, the anonymous role's. openapi-mode = "ignore-privileges" describes everything instead, and "disabled" turns / off. Point Swagger UI, Postman or a code generator at it:

curl localhost:3000/ > openapi.json

Behind a proxy, set openapi-server-proxy-uri to the public URL so the document's servers entry is right.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors are JSON objects in PostgREST's shape:

{
  "code": "23000",
  "message": "violation of FOREIGN KEY constraint INTEG_20 on table ORDERS",
  "details": "Foreign key reference target does not exist\nProblematic key value is (\"CUSTOMER_ID\" = 99)",
  "hint": null
}

code is Firebird's SQLSTATE for database errors, or an FBRST code for API errors. message is the first line of Firebird's message and details the rest.

Status When 300 ambiguous embedding: several foreign keys connect the tables; add a !hint 400 bad query syntax, unknown column, invalid value, constraint or validation error, PSQL EXCEPTION 401 missing, invalid or expired JWT; or permission denied for an anonymous request 403 permission denied for an authenticated role, or the role isn't granted to the database user 404 unknown table, view, procedure or function 405 method not allowed (e.g. PUT without primary key filters) 406 requested media type unavailable, or a single object requested and the row count isn't 1 409 unique or foreign key violation, update conflict, deadlock 416 invalid Range, or (with Prefer: count=exact) an offset beyond the last row 503 the database can't be reached

docs.text: Code Meaning FBRST000 unexpected server error (see the log) FBRST001 the database can't be reached (503) FBRST002 the request took longer than server-request-timeout (503) FBRST100 filter syntax or unknown operator FBRST101 order syntax FBRST102 invalid body or parameter value FBRST103 select syntax, or invalid Range FBRST104 unsupported cast FBRST105 PUT needs eq filters on the whole that isn't in select FBRST109 PATCH/DELETE without filters or limit (db-safe-updates) FBRST114, FBRST115 PUT body doesn't match the URL FBRST116 single object requested, row count isn't 1 FBRST117
