docs.title: Reading tables
docs.text: Every table and view is exposed at /<name>. Global temporary tables are included; system tables are not.

docs.title: Names
docs.text: Firebird stores unquoted identifiers in upper case. The API shows those in lower case, so table BOOKS is /books and column AUTHOR_ID is author_id. Identifiers created with quotes keep their exact spelling: a table "Events Log" is /Events%20Log, with a column "When" as When. Lookups also accept the database spelling (/BOOKS).

docs.title: Selecting columns
docs.text:
Request Meaning GET /books all columns (select=*) GET /books?select=id,title chosen columns, in this order GET /books?select=book:title rename: alias:column GET /books?select=price::text,published::int cast: column::type GET /books?select="Odd Name" quote names that contain special characters

Casts: text, varchar, integer, smallint, bigint, int128, numeric, double, decfloat, boolean, date, time, timestamp.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
A query parameter named after a column filters on it: column=operator.value. Several filters are combined with AND, and one column may be filtered several times (?price=gt.5&price=lt.10).

Operator SQL Example eq, neq =, <> ?status=eq.new gt, gte, lt, lte >, >=, <, <= ?price=lt.10 like LIKE, with * as the wildcard ?title=like.The* ilike case-insensitive LIKE ?title=ilike.*god* similar SIMILAR TO ?code=similar.[A-Z]{3} containing CONTAINING (case-insensitive substring) ?summary=containing.dragon starting STARTING WITH ?title=starting.The in IN (...) ?id=in.(1,2,3), ?name=in.("a,b",c) is IS NULL, IS NOT NULL (not_null), IS TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN ?born=is.null isdistinct IS DISTINCT FROM ?a=isdistinct.5 not.<op> NOT (...) ?id=not.in.(1,2)

containing, starting and similar are Firebird operators that PostgREST does not have. starting can use an index on the column; like/ilike patterns, containing and similar scan the rows.

Values are converted to the column type: booleans accept true/false/t/f/1/0, dates and timestamps accept ISO 8601 (2024-05-06, 2024-05-06T07:08:09Z). Wrap values that contain commas or parentheses in double quotes inside in.(...).

docs.title: Logic trees
docs.text:
or and and take a parenthesised list of conditions written as column.operator.value. They nest, and not. negates a group:

?or=(price.lt.8,and(published.gte.1990,in_stock.is.true))
?not.and=(id.gt.2,id.lt.5)
?or=(title.ilike.*sea*,title.ilike.*star*)
?or=(born.is.null,country.not.eq.UK)

Inside a tree, negate a single condition with column.not.operator.value.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
?order=price.desc
?order=published.desc.nullslast,title
?order=price.asc.nullsfirst

Without order, rows come in whatever order Firebird returns them.

docs.title: Ordering by an embedded resource
docs.text:
Order by a column of a to-one (many-to-one) embed with embed(column). The embed must be in select; use its alias if it has one:

GET /books?select=title,authors(name)&order=authors(name).desc,title
GET /books?select=title,writer:authors(name,born)&order=writer(born)
GET /books?select=title,...authors(name)&order=authors(name)

It works for embedded rows too. This orders each tag's books by their author's name:

GET /tags?select=name,books(title,authors(name))&books.order=authors(name)

Filters on the embed apply: a row whose embed is filtered out, and so returned as null, sorts as NULL. Place those rows with nullsfirst or nullslast.

To-many embeds (one-to-many, many-to-many) have no single value to order by and are refused with FBRST126; order their rows with embed.order= instead (see Resource embedding).

docs.title: Paging
docs.text:
?limit=25&offset=50

or the Range header (items, zero-based, inclusive):

Range: 50-74

Firebird runs these as OFFSET n ROWS FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY. Large offsets get slower, because Firebird has to skip those rows. For deep paging, filter on an indexed key instead (?id=gt.<last id>&order=id&limit=25).

db-max-rows caps every read, whatever the request asks for.

docs.title: Counting
docs.text:
Send Prefer: count=exact to get the total in Content-Range:

GET /books?select=id&limit=2&offset=1
Prefer: count=exact

HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content
Content-Range: 1-2/5

The status is 206 Partial Content when the page doesn't contain every matching row, and 200 otherwise. Counting runs an extra SELECT COUNT(*), which reads every matching row; only ask for it when you need it.

docs.title: Estimated counts
docs.text:
On large tables an exact count is slow, because Firebird has to visit every row. Two cheaper modes return an estimate instead:

Prefer Total in Content-Range count=exact the exact number of matching rows count=planned the table's row count estimated from its index statistics, without reading the table count=estimated exact up to db-max-rows (or 1000 when it is not set), the planned estimate above that

The estimate comes from the statistics of the table's primary key or another unique index: their selectivity is 1 / number of rows. Firebird computes index statistics when an index is created and when you run SET STATISTICS INDEX, so the estimate is as old as that. Recompute them after large loads or deletes, for example in a nightly job. This recomputes every index of the database (in isql, wrap it in SET TERM):

EXECUTE BLOCK AS
  DECLARE name VARCHAR(63);
BEGIN
  FOR SELECT TRIM(RDB$INDEX_NAME) FROM RDB$INDICES WHERE COALESCE(RDB$SYSTEM_FLAG, 0) = 0 INTO :name DO
    EXECUTE STATEMENT 'SET STATISTICS INDEX "' || name || '"';
END

An estimate only describes a whole table. When it doesn't apply, the total is exact and Preference-Applied says count=exact:

  • the request has filters (an estimate of a filtered count would need the optimizer's guesses, which Firebird does not expose);
  • the resource is a view or a procedure;
  • the table has no unique index, or its unique indexes have no statistics yet (an index created on an empty table has none until the next SET STATISTICS);
  • with count=estimated, the estimate is below the rows already counted.

The total is never smaller than the rows in the response: when an old estimate is behind, the rows actually returned win.

docs.title: HEAD
docs.text: HEAD runs the same query and returns only the headers, so HEAD with Prefer: count=exact gives the count without a body.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text: Every request runs in its own transaction. GET and HEAD use a read-only transaction, so a view or selectable procedure that tries to write fails instead of changing data.

docs.title: Procedures and functions
docs.text:
Stored procedures and PSQL functions are called at /rpc/<name>.

Routine Called as Response Selectable procedure (with SUSPEND) SELECT * FROM proc(...) array of rows Executable procedure EXECUTE PROCEDURE proc(...) object of output parameters, or 204 if it has none PSQL function (Firebird 3+) SELECT fn(...) FROM RDB$DATABASE a single JSON value

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
With GET, arguments come from the query string. With POST, they come from a JSON object:

curl 'localhost:3000/rpc/books_by_country?country=UK'
curl -X POST localhost:3000/rpc/place_order -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"customer_id":1,"book_id":2}'
curl 'localhost:3000/rpc/add_vat?amount=100'                 # 119.00
curl 'localhost:3000/rpc/add_vat?amount=100&rate=10'         # 110.00

Arguments are matched by name. A missing argument is NULL, unless it and every argument after it have defaults, in which case the defaults apply (place_order's qty = 1). Unknown argument names in a POST body are rejected.

GET runs in a read-only transaction. Use POST for routines that change data.

docs.title: Calling a routine many times
docs.text:
With Prefer: params=multiple-objects, a POST body that is an array of argument objects calls the routine once per object, in one transaction:

curl -X POST 'localhost:3000/rpc/add_vat' -H 'Prefer: params=multiple-objects' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '[{"amount":100},{"amount":100,"rate":10}]'
# [119.00,110.00]
Routine Response Selectable procedure the rows of every call together, as one result Executable procedure an array with the output parameters of each call, or 204 if it has none PSQL function an array with the value of each call
  • For a selectable procedure the calls are combined into one query (UNION ALL), so select, filters, order, limit and Prefer: count apply to the combined rows: POST /rpc/books_by_country?order=price&limit=5 with [{"country":"UK"},{"country":"USA"}] returns the 5 cheapest books of both countries. Firebird allows 256 procedures per statement, so this takes at most 200 objects (FBRST128); split larger arrays.
  • The calls run in the request's transaction: if one fails, none of them is saved.
  • A single object instead of an array is one call, and the response is still an array.

docs.title: Passing the whole body
docs.text:
With Prefer: params=single-object, the raw JSON body is passed to a routine that has exactly one text parameter (VARCHAR/CHAR or BLOB SUB_TYPE TEXT). Firebird has no JSON type, so the routine receives the JSON document as text, for example to store it:

CREATE PROCEDURE log_request (payload BLOB SUB_TYPE TEXT) RETURNS (id INTEGER) AS
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO api_log (payload) VALUES (:payload) RETURNING id INTO :id;
END

curl -X POST 'localhost:3000/rpc/log_request' -H 'Prefer: params=single-object' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"event":"signup","tags":["a","b"]}'
# {"id":1}

The body must be valid JSON, and fit the parameter when it is a VARCHAR. A routine with another signature is refused with FBRST129.

docs.title: Raw bodies
docs.text:
A POST whose Content-Type is neither JSON nor a form puts the body, as it is, into the routine's only parameter: text/* bodies as text, anything else as bytes. That's the way to upload a file into a BLOB:

curl -X POST localhost:3000/rpc/blob_size -H 'Content-Type: image/png' --data-binary @cover.png \
  -H 'Accept: text/plain'
# 173
curl -X POST localhost:3000/rpc/log_request -H 'Content-Type: text/plain' -d 'plain text, not JSON'

A routine with several parameters gets 400 (FBRST133): send a JSON object instead. The body is limited to 64 MB.

docs.title: Shaping selectable procedures
docs.text:
The output of a selectable procedure can be selected, filtered, ordered, paged and counted like a table. With GET, query parameters that aren't argument names are treated as filters:

GET /rpc/books_by_country?country=UK&select=title&price=lt.9&order=price&limit=1

With POST, the arguments are in the body and the whole query string shapes the result.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Routines declared in a package header are available as /rpc/<package>.<routine>:

CREATE PACKAGE catalog AS
BEGIN
  PROCEDURE search (term VARCHAR(100)) RETURNS (id INTEGER, title VARCHAR(200));
  FUNCTION book_count (author_id INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER;
END

curl 'localhost:3000/rpc/catalog.search?term=god'
curl 'localhost:3000/rpc/catalog.book_count?author_id=1'

Routines that exist only in the package body are private and not exposed.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE books_by_country TO ROLE web_anon;
GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION add_vat TO ROLE web_anon;
GRANT EXECUTE ON PACKAGE catalog TO ROLE web_anon;

-- a routine needs its own rights on the tables it uses
GRANT INSERT ON orders TO PROCEDURE place_order;

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A PSQL EXCEPTION raised by the routine (or by a trigger it fires) becomes a 400 response. The exception's message leads, its name is in hint, and where it was raised is in details:

CREATE EXCEPTION out_of_stock 'This book is out of stock';

-- in the procedure
IF (NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM books b WHERE b.id = :book_id AND b.in_stock)) THEN
  EXCEPTION out_of_stock;

-- Firebird 3+: a routine needs USAGE on the exceptions it raises
GRANT USAGE ON EXCEPTION out_of_stock TO PROCEDURE place_order;

{"code":"HY000","message":"This book is out of stock","details":"At procedure 'PLACE_ORDER' line: 6, col: 5","hint":"exception OUT_OF_STOCK"}

The same applies to exceptions raised by triggers on tables you write to.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text: Send JSON bodies with Content-Type: application/json. A form-urlencoded body is also accepted for a single row.

docs.title: Insert
docs.text:
POST takes one object or an array of objects:

curl -X POST localhost:3000/tags -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"classic"}'
curl -X POST localhost:3000/tags -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '[{"name":"noir"},{"name":"poetry"}]'

The response is 201 Created. For a single row with a primary key, a Location header points to it (/tags?id=eq.7). Columns missing from an object get their default (or the identity value), and unknown keys are rejected with 400.

An array is sent to Firebird in bulk, not row by row. On Firebird 4 and later, a plain insert without Prefer: return=representation uses the wire protocol's batch API: one batch per set of columns, all rows in one message stream. Otherwise (Firebird 3, upserts, a representation wanted, BLOB values, or values the batch can't carry exactly) the rows' statements go in EXECUTE BLOCKs of up to 100 rows, each returning the keys of its rows. Either way a 100-row body costs a few round trips instead of 100. Objects in one array may have different columns. Rows of a view are inserted one by one. If any row fails, the whole request fails and nothing is kept.

docs.title: Getting the rows back
docs.text:
Prefer: return=representation returns the inserted rows, shaped by select, with embeds:

curl -X POST 'localhost:3000/books?select=id,title,authors(name)' \
     -H 'Prefer: return=representation' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '[{"title":"Mort","author_id":1}]'

[{"id":6,"title":"Mort","authors":{"name":"Terry Pratchett"}}]

docs.title: Choosing columns
docs.text:
?columns= lists the keys to insert and ignores the rest. Keys missing from a row become NULL. Add Prefer: missing=default to use the column default instead:

POST /books?columns=title,author_id
Prefer: missing=default

docs.title: Upsert
docs.text:
Prefer Firebird statement On conflict resolution=merge-duplicates UPDATE OR INSERT ... MATCHING (...) update the existing row resolution=ignore-duplicates MERGE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT keep the existing row

Conflicts are detected on the primary key, or on the columns listed in on_conflict:

curl -X POST 'localhost:3000/tags?on_conflict=name' \
     -H 'Prefer: resolution=ignore-duplicates,return=representation' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '[{"name":"fantasy"},{"name":"new-tag"}]'

[{"id":5,"name":"new-tag"}]

With ignore-duplicates, only newly inserted rows are returned.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
PATCH updates every row matching the filters:

curl -X PATCH 'localhost:3000/books?author_id=eq.1&select=id,price' \
     -H 'Prefer: return=representation' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"price":11.50}'

docs.title: Replace one row
docs.text:
PUT with eq filters on every primary key column inserts or replaces that single row. The body must contain the same key values:

curl -X PUT 'localhost:3000/tags?id=eq.10' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"id":10,"name":"noir"}'

docs.title: Delete
docs.text: curl -X DELETE 'localhost:3000/tags?id=eq.10' -H 'Prefer: return=representation'

docs.title: Limiting updates and deletes
docs.text:
limit (and offset) on PATCH or DELETE change only that many of the matching rows. A limit needs an order, so it is clear which rows are picked:

# mark the 10 oldest pending orders as shipped
curl -X PATCH 'localhost:3000/orders?status=eq.pending&order=created_at&limit=10' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"status":"shipped"}'

# delete the 100 oldest log rows, skipping the first 1000
curl -X DELETE 'localhost:3000/audit_log?order=logged_at&offset=1000&limit=100'
  • The order may only use the table's own columns, not an embed's.
  • When the table has a primary key, it is added to the end of the order as a tie-breaker, so rows with equal order values are still picked the same way every time.
  • Prefer: return=representation returns exactly the changed rows, in that order.
  • A limit without an order, or an offset without a limit, is refused with FBRST127.

Firebird runs these as UPDATE … ORDER BY … ROWS m TO n and DELETE … ORDER BY … ROWS m TO n.

docs.title: Capping how many rows a write changes
docs.text:
Prefer: max-affected=n makes a PATCH or DELETE fail, changing nothing, when it would affect more than n rows. As in PostgREST it only applies together with handling=strict:

curl -X DELETE 'localhost:3000/orders?status=eq.cancelled' \
     -H 'Prefer: handling=strict, max-affected=100'

Over the limit the response is 400 with FBRST131 and the number of rows that would have changed; the transaction is rolled back. Use it to guard writes whose filters come from user input.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: PATCH and DELETE without any filter are refused with 400 so a missing parameter can't change a whole table. A limit counts as a restriction: ?order=id&limit=10 is allowed without a filter. Set db-safe-updates = false to allow unrestricted writes.

docs.title: Prefer reference
docs.text:
Prefer Effect return=minimal (default) empty body (201 for POST, 204 for PATCH/PUT/DELETE) return=representation the affected rows, shaped by select count=exact Content-Range ending in /<n>, the number of affected rows resolution=merge-duplicates / ignore-duplicates upsert behaviour of POST missing=default with ?columns=, missing keys use column defaults tx=rollback run the request, then roll back: nothing is saved params=multiple-objects /rpc: call the routine once per object of an array body (details) params=single-object /rpc: pass the whole JSON body to the routine's only text parameter (details) handling=strict refuse the request (FBRST130) if any preference is unknown or invalid; the default lenient ignores them max-affected=n with handling=strict: fail a PATCH/DELETE that would change more than n rows (details) timezone=Europe/Berlin run the request in that time zone (Firebird 4+, details)

Applied preferences are echoed in Preference-Applied. Combine them with commas or several Prefer headers.

docs.title: Value formats
docs.text:
Firebird type JSON SMALLINT, INTEGER, BIGINT number INT128, NUMERIC, DECIMAL, DECFLOAT number, printed exactly as stored (9.99, not 9.9900000001) FLOAT, DOUBLE PRECISION number BOOLEAN true / false DATE "2024-05-06" TIME "13:14:15" TIMESTAMP "2024-05-06T13:14:15.1234" ... WITH TIME ZONE ISO 8601 with offset CHAR, VARCHAR, BLOB SUB_TYPE TEXT string BLOB SUB_TYPE BINARY, OCTETS base64 string (also accepted on input)

On input, ISO 8601 timestamps (2026-10-18T10:00:00+03:00) and JSON numbers or strings for numeric columns are accepted. JSON objects and arrays are stored as their text.

docs.title: Time zones
docs.text:
Prefer: timezone=<IANA name> runs the request in that time zone (Firebird 4+), for reads and writes:

curl 'localhost:3000/meetings?select=title,starts_at' -H 'Prefer: timezone=Asia/Tokyo'
# [{"title":"Release planning","starts_at":"2026-10-20T15:00:00+09:00"}, ...]
  • TIME/TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE values are returned in that zone: the same instant, with the zone's offset. (Firebird stores a zone in each value; without the preference you get the zone it was stored with.)
  • The Firebird session uses the zone too (SET TIME ZONE): CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, column defaults, and timestamps without an offset in filters or bodies (starts_at=eq.2026-10-20T15:00:00) are in that zone. The session zone is reset before the connection goes back to the pool.
  • Plain TIME and TIMESTAMP columns have no zone and are not converted.
  • An unknown zone is ignored (it is missing from Preference-Applied); with handling=strict it is refused with FBRST130. Firebird 3 has no time zones, so there the preference is ignored.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings come from an optional config file passed as the only argument, and from FBREST_* environment variables. Environment variables override the file.

firebirdrest /etc/firebirdrest.conf
FBREST_DB_POOL=20 firebirdrest /etc/firebirdrest.conf

The file holds key = value lines; values may be quoted, and # starts a comment. Unknown keys are an error, so typos don't go unnoticed. A complete example is in examples/firebirdrest.conf.

db-uri = "authenticator:secret@localhost:3050/var/lib/firebird/data/app.fdb"
db-anon-role = "web_anon"
jwt-secret = "a long random string of at least 32 characters"

docs.title: Database
docs.text: Key Environment Default db-uri FBREST_DB_URI (required) user:password@host[:port]/path/to/db.fdb[?options] db-anon-role FBREST_DB_ANON_ROLE none role for requests without a JWT; empty means a token is required db-pool FBREST_DB_POOL 10 connections per role db-max-rows FBREST_DB_MAX_ROWS 0 maximum rows per read (0 = no limit); also where Prefer: count=estimated switches to the estimate (1000 when 0) db-pre-request FBREST_DB_PRE_REQUEST none executable procedure run at the start of each request (proc or schema.proc) db-safe-updates FBREST_DB_SAFE_UPDATES true refuse PATCH/DELETE without filters or limit db-aggregates-enabled FBREST_DB_AGGREGATES_ENABLED true allow count(), sum(), … db-plan-enabled FBREST_DB_PLAN_ENABLED false allow Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.plan (query plans) db-schemas FBREST_DB_SCHEMAS public Firebird 6+, experimental: comma-separated SQL schemas to expose, the first is the default (schemas) db-request-context FBREST_DB_REQUEST_CONTEXT auto when to set request.* variables: auto, always, never (details) db-prepared-statements FBREST_DB_PREPARED_STATEMENTS 256 prepared statements cached per role (0 = off) db-prepared-statements-idle FBREST_DB_PREPARED_STATEMENTS_IDLE 30 seconds after which an unused cached statement is closed (why) db-read-tx-reuse FBREST_DB_READ_TX_REUSE true GET/HEAD requests share long-lived read-only transactions, one per connection, instead of starting and committing one each (details) db-reload-event FBREST_DB_RELOAD_EVENT fbrest_reload POST_EVENT name that reloads the schema cache; empty disables it

docs.title: db-uri options
docs.text:
The URI is passed to the nakagami/firebirdsql driver. Useful options:

Option Default charset UTF8 connection character set wire_crypt true encrypt the connection (Firebird 3+); false for servers with WireCrypt = Disabled auth_plugin_name Srp256 Srp, Srp256 or Legacy_Auth timezone server's time zone for TIMESTAMP/TIME without zone wire_compress false compress the wire protocol, useful over slow links 
db-uri = "authenticator:secret@db.internal:3050/data/app.fdb?wire_crypt=false&charset=UTF8"

Don't add role= yourself: FirebirdREST sets the role per request.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Key Environment Default jwt-secret FBREST_JWT_SECRET none HMAC secret, PEM public key or certificate, JWK or JWKS; @/path reads it from a file (formats) jwt-secret-is-base64 FBREST_JWT_SECRET_IS_BASE64 false the HMAC secret is base64 encoded jwt-jwks-url FBREST_JWT_JWKS_URL none JWKS of an identity provider, fetched over HTTP(S) and refreshed (details) jwt-jwks-refresh FBREST_JWT_JWKS_REFRESH 3600 seconds between fetches of jwt-jwks-url (minimum 30) jwt-cache-max-entries FBREST_JWT_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES 1000 accepted tokens remembered to skip signature checks; 0 disables the cache jwt-aud FBREST_JWT_AUD none required aud claim jwt-role-claim-key FBREST_JWT_ROLE_CLAIM_KEY role claim holding the role; dots for nested claims (app_metadata.role)

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
Key Environment Default server-host FBREST_SERVER_HOST 0.0.0.0 listen address server-port FBREST_SERVER_PORT 3000 API port server-request-timeout FBREST_SERVER_REQUEST_TIMEOUT 60 seconds a request may take to arrive and to be handled; 0 disables (details) server-max-body-size FBREST_SERVER_MAX_BODY_SIZE 16 largest request body, in MB (413 above it) server-cors-allowed-origins FBREST_SERVER_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS * comma-separated origins allowed by CORS; * allows any origin without credentials; empty disables CORS headers openapi-server-proxy-uri FBREST_OPENAPI_SERVER_PROXY_URI request host public URL shown in the OpenAPI document openapi-mode FBREST_OPENAPI_MODE follow-privileges what GET / describes: only what the caller's role is granted (follow-privileges), everything (ignore-privileges), or nothing (disabled, 404) server-timing-enabled FBREST_SERVER_TIMING_ENABLED false add a Server-Timing header to responses (details) admin-server-port FBREST_ADMIN_SERVER_PORT 0 (off) admin server: GET /live, GET /ready, POST /reload, GET /metrics admin-server-host FBREST_ADMIN_SERVER_HOST server-host listen address of the admin server, e.g. 127.0.0.1 admin-pprof FBREST_ADMIN_PPROF false serve Go profiling at /debug/pprof/ on the admin port log-level FBREST_LOG_LEVEL info debug, info, warn or error; info logs every request

The admin server has no authentication. Don't expose it publicly: anyone who can reach it can reload the schema cache, read the metrics, and with admin-pprof read profiling data. Bind it to a private interface with admin-server-host, or keep it off the public port mapping.

Boolean settings left empty in the config file (admin-pprof =) keep their default.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
firebirdrest [config-file]
firebirdrest -version
firebirdrest -check [config-file]

-check loads the configuration, prints warnings (deprecated settings, a short jwt-secret, the CORS wildcard, no way to authenticate) and exits with status 0, or with status 2 and the error when a setting is unknown or invalid. Nothing is connected. Use it before a rollout; see Upgrading. The same warnings are logged at startup.

FirebirdREST retries the database connection with back-off until it succeeds, so it can start before Firebird. It stops gracefully on SIGINT/SIGTERM and reloads the schema cache on SIGUSR1 (not on Windows).

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: FirebirdREST is one static binary with no dependencies. Run it close to the database: every request makes a few round trips, so latency between the two adds up.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
docker run -d --name firebirdrest -p 3000:3000 -p 3001:3001 \
  -e FBREST_DB_URI='authenticator:secret@db.internal:3050/data/app.fdb' \
  -e FBREST_DB_ANON_ROLE=web_anon \
  -e FBREST_JWT_SECRET="$(cat /run/secrets/jwt_secret)" \
  -e FBREST_ADMIN_SERVER_PORT=3001 \
  ghcr.io/mariuz/firebirdrest:latest

Images are published for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 with tags latest, X.Y and X.Y.Z. They are based on distroless and run as a non-root user.

docker-compose.yml in the repository runs Firebird, FirebirdREST and Swagger UI together.

docs.title: systemd
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/firebirdrest.service
[Unit]
Description=FirebirdREST
After=network-online.target firebird.service
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/firebirdrest /etc/firebirdrest.conf
ExecReload=/bin/kill -USR1 $MAINPID
Restart=on-failure
DynamicUser=yes
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

systemctl reload firebirdrest then reloads the schema cache.

docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy
docs.text:
Put TLS and rate limiting in front of FirebirdREST, for example with nginx:

location /api/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000/;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
}

Set openapi-server-proxy-uri = "https://example.com/api" so the OpenAPI document shows the public URL. X-Forwarded-For is available to PSQL as request.header.x-forwarded-for.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
With admin-server-port set:

Endpoint GET /live 200 while the process runs GET /ready 200 when the database answers, 503 otherwise POST /reload reload the schema cache (204) GET /metrics metrics in the Prometheus format (list) 
# Kubernetes
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /live,  port: 3001 } }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 3001 } }

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
• db-pool is per role. With several roles in use, the database sees up to roles × db-pool connections from each FirebirdREST instance.
  • FirebirdREST keeps no state besides its caches, so you can run several instances behind a load balancer. Reload each one after DDL; the POST_EVENT route reaches all of them at once.
  • See Benchmarks for throughput figures and the load tool.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: Download the new binary or pull the new image and restart. Settings and behaviour changes are listed in the changelog.

docs.title: Firebird 6
docs.text:
Firebird 6 is not released yet. CI runs the full integration suite against the nightly firebirdsql/firebird:6-snapshot image on every push and once a week, so problems show up before the release. Firebird 6 adds SQL schemas, which FirebirdREST can expose with db-schemas (see Schemas); by default it serves PUBLIC.

Known issue with the current snapshot: text columns declared CHARACTER SET NONE (the default in a database created without DEFAULT CHARACTER SET) fail with string right truncation once a value is longer than a quarter of the column's size, when the client connects as UTF8 (FirebirdREST's default). Firebird 6 reads the row buffer the driver asks for as UTF8 characters (4 bytes each) instead of bytes, as Firebird 5 does. A fix in the Go driver FirebirdREST uses, which sizes that buffer for the connection character set, is proposed in nakagami/firebirdsql#317. The Python driver firebirdsql has the same problem and the same fix, proposed in nakagami/pyfirebirdsql#142. Until a driver release includes it, either create the database with a character set:

CREATE DATABASE 'app.fdb' DEFAULT CHARACTER SET UTF8;

or connect with the database's own character set, for example db-uri = "user:pass@host/app.fdb?charset=NONE".

A second issue of the same kind affects binary data: with the current driver, Firebird 6 refuses to read CHARACTER SET OCTETS columns and to write binary values under 32 KB (into BLOB SUB_TYPE BINARY or OCTETS columns) with Malformed string, because it validates them as UTF8 text. BLOB SUB_TYPE BINARY reads, and writes of 32 KB and more, work. The driver fix is on the branch fix-fb6-octets, being sent upstream.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: FirebirdREST reports what it's doing in three ways: metrics in the Prometheus format on the admin port, an optional Server-Timing header on each response, and a log line per request.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
With admin-server-port set, GET /metrics on the admin port returns metrics in the Prometheus text format:

curl -s localhost:3001/metrics | grep requests_total
# firebirdrest_requests_total{method="GET",status="200"} 1832
# firebirdrest_requests_total{method="POST",status="201"} 41

A Prometheus scrape job:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: firebirdrest
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["firebirdrest:3001"]

In Kubernetes, scrape the admin port of each pod; don't route it through the public service.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels firebirdrest_requests_total counter method, status requests served firebirdrest_request_duration_seconds histogram method time to serve a request, from 1 ms to 10 s buckets firebirdrest_errors_total counter code error responses by code: FBRST... or the Firebird SQLSTATE (see errors)

method is one of GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS or OTHER.

docs.title: Connection pools and statement caches
docs.text:
Each Firebird role has its own pool and statement cache; these metrics have a role label, with the role name in upper case as Firebird stores it. The pool with an empty role is the connection without a role that reads the schema cache.

Metric Type firebirdrest_db_pool_max_connections gauge db-pool firebirdrest_db_pool_open_connections gauge open connections, in use or idle firebirdrest_db_pool_in_use_connections gauge connections running a request firebirdrest_db_pool_idle_connections gauge idle connections firebirdrest_db_pool_waits_total counter times a request waited for a free connection firebirdrest_db_pool_wait_seconds_total counter total time spent waiting firebirdrest_stmt_cache_hits_total counter statements run from the prepared statement cache firebirdrest_stmt_cache_misses_total counter statements that had to be prepared firebirdrest_stmt_cache_entries gauge statements in the cache

A rising firebirdrest_db_pool_waits_total means requests queue for connections: raise db-pool, or check for slow queries. The statement cache metrics are absent with db-prepared-statements = 0.

docs.title: Schema cache
docs.text: Metric Type firebirdrest_schema_reloads_total counter schema cache loads, the first one included firebirdrest_schema_reload_errors_total counter failed loads (the previous cache stays in use) firebirdrest_schema_load_duration_seconds gauge how long the last successful load took firebirdrest_schema_load_time_seconds gauge when it happened, in unix seconds firebirdrest_schema_relations gauge tables and views, by schema firebirdrest_schema_routines gauge procedures and functions, by schema

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Metric Type firebirdrest_jwt_cache_hits_total counter tokens found in the validation cache firebirdrest_jwt_cache_misses_total counter tokens whose signature was checked firebirdrest_jwks_fetches_total counter fetches of jwt-jwks-url (only with it set) firebirdrest_jwks_fetch_errors_total counter failed fetches

docs.title: Process
docs.text: Metric Type firebirdrest_build_info gauge always 1; version and firebird (server version) labels firebirdrest_start_time_seconds gauge process start, in unix seconds go_goroutines gauge goroutines go_memstats_heap_alloc_bytes gauge heap in use go_memstats_sys_bytes gauge memory obtained from the operating system go_gc_cycles_total counter garbage collections

docs.title: Example alerts
docs.text:
groups:
  - name: firebirdrest
    rules:
      - alert: FirebirdRESTErrors
        expr: sum(rate(firebirdrest_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) > 0.1
      - alert: FirebirdRESTSlow
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(firebirdrest_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 0.5
      - alert: FirebirdRESTPoolSaturated
        expr: rate(firebirdrest_db_pool_waits_total[5m]) > 1
      - alert: FirebirdRESTSchemaReloadFailed
        expr: increase(firebirdrest_schema_reload_errors_total[15m]) > 0

docs.title: Server-Timing
docs.text:
With server-timing-enabled = true, responses carry a Server-Timing header, as in PostgREST. Browser developer tools show it in the network panel's Timing tab.

Server-Timing: jwt;dur=0.1, parse;dur=0.2, transaction;dur=3.4, response;dur=0.3
Name Time spent (milliseconds) jwt verifying the bearer token parse parsing the URL and the body, and building the SQL transaction in the database: from BEGIN to COMMIT, less parse and response response rendering the result as JSON, CSV or text

Error responses have no Server-Timing header. The header shows how your API is built, so leave it off on public APIs unless you want clients to see it.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Each request is logged at info level with method, path, status and duration, as text on standard error:

time=2026-10-20T18:12:01.123Z level=INFO msg=request method=GET path=/books status=200 took=1.84ms

log-level = warn keeps only problems, such as a failed schema reload or JWKS fetch.

docs.title: Schema cache
docs.text:
At start-up FirebirdREST reads the Firebird system tables (RDB$RELATIONS, RDB$RELATION_FIELDS, RDB$RELATION_CONSTRAINTS, RDB$PROCEDURES, RDB$FUNCTIONS and friends) and keeps the tables, columns, keys, foreign keys, routines and computed relationships in memory. Requests are validated and planned from this cache, so it has to be reloaded after DDL.

level=INFO msg="schema cache loaded" firebird=5.0.4 relations=8 routines=10 foreign_keys=6 request_context=true took=39ms

docs.title: Reloading
docs.text:
Any of these reloads it without dropping requests in flight:

From the databaseSignalAdmin server 
-- in isql; other tools don't need SET TERM
SET TERM ^;
EXECUTE BLOCK AS BEGIN POST_EVENT 'fbrest_reload'; END^
SET TERM ;^
COMMIT;

Firebird delivers the event when the transaction commits. The name is set by db-reload-event.

kill -USR1 $(pidof firebirdrest)

curl -X POST localhost:3001/reload        # with admin-server-port = 3001

docs.title: Reloading automatically after DDL
docs.text:
A database-level DDL trigger (Firebird 3+) posts the event after every metadata change:

SET TERM ^;
CREATE TRIGGER fbrest_ddl_reload AFTER ANY DDL STATEMENT AS
BEGIN
  POST_EVENT 'fbrest_reload';
END^
SET TERM ;^

docs.title: DDL and cached statements
docs.text:
FirebirdREST also caches prepared statements (db-prepared-statements), which roughly halves the cost of each query. Firebird keeps a lock on every table, view and routine a prepared statement refers to:

DDL While statements are cached ALTER TABLE ... ADD / DROP column, CREATE OR ALTER VIEW / PROCEDURE works DROP TABLE, DROP VIEW, DROP PROCEDURE, ... waits until the statements using the object are closed

Statements unused for db-prepared-statements-idle seconds (default 30) are closed, and every reload closes all of them. To drop an object that is in active use, reload first and then run the DROP straight away:

curl -X POST localhost:3001/reload && isql -i drop_things.sql ...

Or set db-prepared-statements = 0 to turn the statement cache off.

docs.title: Schemas
docs.text:
Experimental

Schema support is built and tested against the Firebird 6 snapshot, before Firebird 6 is released. The configuration and headers follow PostgREST and are expected to stay, but details may change if Firebird 6 changes before its release.

Firebird 6 adds SQL schemas: named namespaces for tables, views, procedures, functions and packages, like PostgreSQL's. FirebirdREST can expose several of them and lets each request pick one, with the same headers as PostgREST.

Firebird 3, 4 and 5 have no schemas: the whole database is one namespace, db-schemas must not be set, and the profile headers below are answered with 406.

docs.title: Exposing schemas
docs.text:
db-schemas = "public, inventory"

The first schema is the default. Without db-schemas, Firebird 6 exposes PUBLIC only, as before. Names are matched like unquoted identifiers (inventory is INVENTORY); a schema created with a quoted, mixed-case name is written as stored. FirebirdREST refuses to start if a schema doesn't exist, and SYSTEM cannot be exposed.

Each schema has its own schema cache, reloaded together by POST_EVENT 'fbrest_reload' or POST /reload.

docs.title: Choosing the schema of a request
docs.text:
Request Header GET, HEAD Accept-Profile: inventory POST, PATCH, PUT, DELETE Content-Profile: inventory 
curl 'localhost:3000/warehouses?select=name,stock(qty)' -H 'Accept-Profile: inventory'
curl -X POST 'localhost:3000/warehouses' -H 'Content-Profile: inventory' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Iasi"}'
curl 'localhost:3000/rpc/low_stock?below=5' -H 'Accept-Profile: inventory'

Without a header the request uses the default schema. With more than one schema exposed, every response says which one it used in Content-Profile. A schema that isn't exposed is refused with 406 (FBRST106), listing the exposed ones. The OpenAPI description at / follows Accept-Profile too.

Everything in a request happens in its schema:

  • tables, views and routines are looked up there, so two schemas can each have a books table;
  • every statement uses schema-qualified names ("INVENTORY"."STOCK"), not the search path;
  • embedding follows foreign keys within the schema and into the other exposed schemas (see below); computed fields and relationships only use routines and TYPE OF COLUMN parameters of the same schema;
  • packaged routines are /rpc/package.name of the schema's packages.

docs.title: Relationships across schemas
docs.text:
A foreign key whose table and referenced table are in two exposed schemas is a relationship like any other, in both directions, as in PostgREST. In the example, inventory.stock.book_id references public.books:

# from inventory into public ...
curl 'localhost:3000/stock?select=qty,books(title)' -H 'Accept-Profile: inventory'
# ... and from public into inventory, nesting on within inventory
curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=title,stock(qty,warehouses(name))&id=eq.1'

The embedded table is named as in its own schema; it does not become a resource of the request's schema (GET /stock without Accept-Profile: inventory is still 404). When the request's schema has a table of the same name, as inventory has its own books, the foreign key decides which one is meant; with several candidate keys, disambiguate with books!<constraint or column>(...) as usual. A foreign key into a schema that is not in db-schemas is not a relationship: that table is not part of the API.

The role needs USAGE on both schemas and the usual SELECT on the embedded table.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Besides the grants on each object, a role needs USAGE on the schema (for PUBLIC this is granted to everyone by default):

GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA inventory TO ROLE web_anon;
GRANT SELECT ON inventory.warehouses TO ROLE web_anon;

Without it every request into the schema fails with no permission for USAGE access to SCHEMA, answered as 401 for anonymous requests and 403 otherwise.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
examples/bookstore-fb6.sql adds an inventory schema to the example database, with warehouses, stock, its own books table, a selectable procedure, a package and the grants above.

db-pre-request may name a procedure of any schema: db-pre-request = "inventory.check_request".

docs.title: Security and roles
docs.text: FirebirdREST follows PostgREST's model: it authenticates requests, then leaves authorization to the database.

docs.title: The authenticator user and roles
docs.text:
1. FirebirdREST logs in as one database user, the authenticator, which has no privileges of its own.
  2. Each request runs in its own transaction under a Firebird role: the JWT's role claim, or db-anon-role for requests without a token.
  3. The GRANTs on tables, views, procedures, functions and packages for that role decide what the request may do. A refused statement becomes 401 (anonymous) or 403 (authenticated).
CREATE USER authenticator PASSWORD 'a long random password';

CREATE ROLE web_anon;
CREATE ROLE web_user;

GRANT SELECT ON books TO ROLE web_anon;
GRANT ALL    ON books TO ROLE web_user;
GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE place_order TO ROLE web_user;

GRANT web_anon TO USER authenticator;
GRANT web_user TO USER authenticator;

Don't connect as SYSDBA or the database owner

In Firebird, SYSDBA, the database owner and users with the RDB$ADMIN role bypass every grant: every request would be able to read and change everything. Create a separate user. Note that the official Docker image makes FIREBIRD_USER the owner of the database it creates.

Firebird silently ignores a role that hasn't been granted to the connecting user and carries on with no role. FirebirdREST checks CURRENT_ROLE when it opens a role's connection pool and refuses requests for such roles with 403 FBRST300.

Each role gets its own connection pool of db-pool connections, opened when the role is first used.

docs.title: JSON Web Tokens
docs.text:
Send Authorization: Bearer <token>. The token is verified with the keys of jwt-secret, jwt-jwks-url, or both:

jwt-secret Algorithms a string (32+ characters recommended) HS256, HS384, HS512 the same, base64 encoded, with jwt-secret-is-base64 = true HS256, HS384, HS512 a PEM public key or certificate (-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----, -----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY----- or -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----); several blocks give several keys RSA: RS256/384/512, PS256/384/512; ECDSA: ES256/384/512; Ed25519: EdDSA a JWK ({"kty": "RSA", ...}) or a JWKS ({"keys": [...]}) as JSON as for PEM, plus HS* for "kty": "oct" keys @/path/to/file: any of the above, read from the file at startup

A key only verifies tokens of its own type: an RSA key never accepts an HS256 token, so a public key can't be misused as an HMAC secret. A JWK with alg accepts only that algorithm, and JWKS entries with "use": "enc" are ignored. When the token names a key with kid, only keys with that kid (or without one) are tried; otherwise every key of the right type is.

Secret files

An @file HMAC secret is used byte for byte, including a trailing newline if the file has one. Write it with printf '%s' "$SECRET" > file, or use base64 and jwt-secret-is-base64.

docs.title: Keys from an identity provider
docs.text:
Identity providers such as Auth0, Keycloak, Okta, Azure AD or Google publish their signing keys as a JWKS at a URL, and rotate them. Point jwt-jwks-url at it:

jwt-jwks-url = "https://example.eu.auth0.com/.well-known/jwks.json"
jwt-aud = "https://api.example.com"
jwt-role-claim-key = "https://example.com/role"

FirebirdREST fetches the URL at startup and every jwt-jwks-refresh seconds (default 3600). A token whose kid isn't known yet triggers an extra fetch, at most once every 30 seconds, so a newly rotated key works right away. If a fetch fails the previous keys stay in use; if the first fetch fails, FirebirdREST starts anyway (anonymous requests keep working) and retries every 30 seconds. A key that disappears from the JWKS stops working as soon as the change is fetched.

docs.title: Validation cache
docs.text:
Checking an RSA or ECDSA signature costs far more than the rest of the authentication, so accepted tokens are remembered: up to jwt-cache-max-entries tokens (default 1000; 0 turns the cache off), each until its exp or for 5 minutes, whichever is sooner. The cache is emptied when the JWKS keys change and when the schema cache reloads. Rejected tokens are never cached.

exp and nbf are checked when present. With jwt-aud set, the aud claim must match.

The role is read from the role claim. Use jwt-role-claim-key for another place, with dots for nested claims:

jwt-role-claim-key = "app_metadata.role"

A valid token without a role claim uses db-anon-role. Role names must be plain identifiers ([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_$]*).

Problem Response no token and no db-anon-role 401 FBRST302 malformed, badly signed, expired or wrong audience 401 FBRST301 role not granted to the authenticator 403 FBRST300 token sent but neither jwt-secret nor jwt-jwks-url configured 500 FBRST300 no key for the token's algorithm or kid 401 FBRST301

docs.title: Request context in PSQL
docs.text:
Request data is available to views, triggers, procedures, functions and check constraints as transaction-scoped context variables in the USER_TRANSACTION namespace:

Variable Value request.role Firebird role of the request request.method, request.path HTTP method and path request.jwt.claim.<name> each string, number or boolean claim, e.g. request.jwt.claim.sub request.jwt.claims the whole claims object as JSON, if it fits in 255 characters request.header.origin, request.header.user-agent, request.header.x-forwarded-for those headers, when sent 
SELECT RDB$GET_CONTEXT('USER_TRANSACTION', 'request.jwt.claim.sub') FROM RDB$DATABASE

Values longer than 255 characters are truncated (a Firebird limit).

docs.title: Row-level security
docs.text:
Combine the context with views and triggers:

-- users only see their own orders
CREATE VIEW my_orders AS
  SELECT o.* FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE c.email = RDB$GET_CONTEXT('USER_TRANSACTION', 'request.jwt.claim.sub');

-- and can only create orders for themselves
CREATE EXCEPTION not_your_customer 'You can only order for yourself';

SET TERM ^;
CREATE TRIGGER orders_owner FOR orders BEFORE INSERT AS
BEGIN
  IF (NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.id = NEW.customer_id
        AND c.email = RDB$GET_CONTEXT('USER_TRANSACTION', 'request.jwt.claim.sub'))) THEN
    EXCEPTION not_your_customer;
END^
SET TERM ;^

GRANT USAGE ON EXCEPTION not_your_customer TO TRIGGER orders_owner;
GRANT SELECT ON customers TO TRIGGER orders_owner;

docs.title: When the variables are set
docs.text:
Setting the variables costs a database round trip, so by default (db-request-context = auto) FirebirdREST only does it when some object in the database could read them. At each schema load it searches the source of every view, trigger, procedure, function and package, and every computed, default and check expression, for the text request.. Routines whose source is not stored also count as possible readers. The schema cache loaded log line shows the outcome as request_context=true or false.

Use db-request-context = always if you read the variables from code FirebirdREST can't see (for example a UDR written in C++, or dynamic SQL that builds the names), or never to skip them entirely.

docs.title: Pre-request procedure
docs.text:
db-pre-request names an executable procedure that runs at the start of every request, after the context variables are set. Raise an exception to reject the request:

CREATE EXCEPTION banned 'This account is suspended';

SET TERM ^;
CREATE PROCEDURE check_request AS
BEGIN
  IF (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM banned_users
        WHERE email = RDB$GET_CONTEXT('USER_TRANSACTION', 'request.jwt.claim.sub'))) THEN
    EXCEPTION banned;
END^
SET TERM ;^

GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE check_request TO ROLE web_anon;
GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE check_request TO ROLE web_user;
GRANT SELECT ON banned_users TO PROCEDURE check_request;
GRANT USAGE ON EXCEPTION banned TO PROCEDURE check_request;

db-pre-request = "check_request"

A banned user's requests then fail with 400 {"message":"This account is suspended","hint":"exception BANNED",...}.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text: Every write runs in its own transaction, committed when the request succeeds and rolled back otherwise. Reads (GET, HEAD) run in read-only READ COMMITTED transactions that are reused: each connection of a role keeps one open and serves request after request with it. A statement in such a transaction sees the data committed when the statement starts, exactly as it would in a transaction of its own, so responses are the same; what's saved is the transaction start and commit round trips of every read. Firebird treats read-only read-committed transactions as pre-committed, so the long-lived ones don't hold back garbage collection. They are recycled after 1000 requests or 5 minutes, and request context variables set by one request are cleared by the next. db-read-tx-reuse = false gives every read its own transaction. Query plan requests always use a fresh transaction.

docs.title: Other safeguards
docs.text:
• PATCH and DELETE without filters are refused (db-safe-updates).
  • GET and HEAD run in read-only transactions.
  • db-max-rows caps the rows a single read can return.
  • Identifiers from the URL are checked against the schema cache and always quoted; values are always sent as parameters, never inlined into SQL.
  • Error responses never carry the database login, host or internal error text: Firebird's "Effective user is ..." line is removed, and unexpected errors return a generic message while the cause goes to the log.
  • The OpenAPI document at / lists only what the caller's role may use (openapi-mode).

docs.title: Request limits
docs.text:
A request is bounded in time and size, so one client can't tie up the server:

Limit Setting Time to send and handle a request 60 s server-request-timeout (503 FBRST002 when exceeded) Request body 16 MB server-max-body-size (413 FBRST134) Request line and headers 64 KB fixed and=/or= nesting 16 levels fixed (400) Values in one in.() filter 1000 fixed (400) Objects in Prefer: params=multiple-objects for a selectable procedure 200 fixed (400 FBRST128)

The body is read in full before the transaction starts, so a slow client never holds a database connection while sending.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text: server-cors-allowed-origins = "*" (the default) answers any origin with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and no credentials, which is enough for bearer tokens set by JavaScript. To let browsers send credentials (cookies, HTTP auth from a proxy in front), list the origins explicitly: each is reflected with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and Vary: Origin. An empty value turns the CORS headers off.

docs.title: Responses as data
docs.text: Every response carries X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox, so a browser never treats a value stored in the database as a page of the API's origin. A single value requested as text/html, SVG, XML, JavaScript or PDF is sent with Content-Disposition: attachment: it downloads instead of rendering.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Role names from tokens are folded to upper case, as Firebird folds unquoted identifiers, so web_user and WEB_USER share one connection pool. Only roles the authenticator is granted get a pool; the check happens when the pool is opened.

docs.title: Stability promise
docs.text: What you can build on, what may still change, and how changes are announced. FirebirdREST follows semantic versioning: until 1.0 a minor version (0.x → 0.y) may change behaviour, and every such change is listed under behaviour changes at the top of the version's changelog entry. From 1.0 on, the interfaces marked stable below change only in a major version.

docs.title: Stable
docs.text:
These are the interfaces applications depend on. They are covered by the test suite on Firebird 3, 4 and 5, and by the firebirdrest-js compatibility suite.

Interface What is promised URL grammar select, filters and operators, order, limit/offset, logic trees, embedding (!inner, !hint, spread), aggregates, casts, /rpc/<name> and /rpc/<package>.<name>, as documented in the API. New operators and parameters may be added; existing ones keep their meaning. Request headers Prefer values, Range, Accept media types, Accept-Profile/Content-Profile, Authorization: Bearer. Response headers Content-Range, Range-Unit, Preference-Applied, Content-Profile, Location, Content-Type. The nosniff/CSP security headers stay. Status codes As listed in errors. Error body {code, message, details, hint}. FBRST codes are never reused for another meaning; a code may be retired, never redefined. Firebird errors keep Firebird's SQLSTATE as code. message text may be reworded. JSON encoding of types numbers as JSON numbers (exact numerics as numbers, not strings), BOOLEAN as booleans, dates and times as ISO 8601 strings, WITH TIME ZONE values with their offset, binary as base64, BLOB SUB_TYPE TEXT as strings. Request context variables the request.* names available to PSQL through RDB$GET_CONTEXT. Configuration every key in the configuration reference, its FBREST_* environment variable, and its default. A default changes only in a minor version before 1.0, in a major one after. Admin endpoints /live, /ready, /reload, /metrics. Metric names firebirdrest_* metrics and their labels. Metrics may be added. Command line firebirdrest [config-file], -version, -check. Docker image ghcr.io/mariuz/firebirdrest with tags X.Y.Z, X.Y and latest, running as a non-root user on port 3000, configured through FBREST_*. Firebird versions 3.0, 4.0 and 5.0. A Firebird version is dropped only in a major release, after its vendor end of life.

docs.title: Experimental
docs.text:
Available and tested, but may change in a minor version while the ground under it moves. Each is marked as such in its documentation.

Feature Why SQL schemas (db-schemas, Accept-Profile on Firebird 6) Firebird 6 is not released; its schema catalog may still change. Firebird 6 support in general Tested against the nightly snapshot in CI, with known driver issues listed under Deployment. Query plan output (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.plan) The text is Firebird's explained plan, which differs between Firebird versions; the JSON shape [{query, plan}] is stable, the plan text is not. Server-Timing metric names Follow PostgREST's; may gain entries.

docs.title: Not covered
docs.text:
• The exact text of message, details and hint in errors, and of Firebird's own messages.
  • The format of log lines.
  • The OpenAPI document's descriptions and the order of its entries (its structure follows the OpenAPI 3.0 specification).
  • The Go packages under internal/: FirebirdREST is a program, not a library.
  • Statement text shown in query plans.
  • Undocumented behaviour. If you rely on something that isn't documented, open an issue so it can be documented or changed deliberately.

docs.title: How changes are made
docs.text:
• Additions (a new operator, header, setting, metric or error code) can arrive in any release and are listed under Added.
  • Behaviour changes are listed first in the version's changelog entry, under behaviour changes to check before upgrading, with the setting that restores the old behaviour when there is one.
  • Deprecations: a setting or feature to be removed keeps working for at least one minor version while the server logs a warning at startup naming its replacement. Renamed settings accept the old name during that time.
  • Removals happen in a major version (or, before 1.0, in a minor version after the deprecation period), and are listed under Removed.
  • Security fixes may change behaviour in a patch release when the old behaviour is the vulnerability; the changelog says so.

Before deploying a new version, run the binary with -check against your configuration: it loads the configuration, reports unknown or invalid settings and deprecation warnings, and exits without connecting to the database. See the upgrade guide.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: This tutorial continues from Getting started. You'll make a JSON Web Token (JWT) for the web_user role, use it to write data, and then use one of its claims inside the database.

docs.title: How requests get a role
docs.text:
FirebirdREST connects as the user authenticator, which has no privileges of its own. For every request it opens a transaction under a Firebird role:

  • with no Authorization header: the anonymous role, db-anon-role (web_anon in the example);
  • with Authorization: Bearer <JWT>: the role named in the token's role claim.

Firebird's GRANTs for that role then decide what the request may do. The example grants web_anon read access to the catalogue and web_user everything:

GRANT SELECT ON books TO ROLE web_anon;
GRANT ALL    ON books TO ROLE web_user;
GRANT ALL    ON orders TO ROLE web_user;

GRANT web_anon TO USER authenticator;
GRANT web_user TO USER authenticator;

docs.title: 1. Make a token
docs.text:
The token is signed with the secret in jwt-secret. docker-compose sets it to reallyreallyreallyreallyverysafe1234. In production use a long random value.

Any JWT library works. With plain shell tools:

SECRET='reallyreallyreallyreallyverysafe1234'
b64() { base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=\n'; }
header=$(printf '{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}' | b64)
payload=$(printf '{"role":"web_user","sub":"ana@example.com","exp":%d}' $(( $(date +%s) + 3600 )) | b64)
signature=$(printf '%s.%s' "$header" "$payload" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET" -binary | b64)
TOKEN="$header.$payload.$signature"

The token expires in an hour (exp). FirebirdREST rejects expired tokens with 401.

docs.title: 2. Use it
docs.text:
curl localhost:3000/customers -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

[{"id":1,"email":"ana@example.com","name":"Ana"},{"id":2,"email":"bob@example.com","name":"Bob"}]

Without the header, the same request gets 401, because web_anon has no grant on customers.

Now the write that failed before:

curl -X POST 'localhost:3000/tags?select=id,name' \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Prefer: return=representation' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"classic"}'

[{"id":4,"name":"classic"}]

And an executable procedure that creates an order:

curl -X POST localhost:3000/rpc/place_order -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"customer_id":1,"book_id":2}'

{"order_id":2}

docs.title: 3. Read claims inside the database
docs.text:
Every scalar claim is available to PSQL as a transaction context variable. The example function whoami reads the sub claim:

CREATE FUNCTION whoami RETURNS VARCHAR(255) AS
BEGIN
  RETURN COALESCE(RDB$GET_CONTEXT('USER_TRANSACTION', 'request.jwt.claim.sub'), 'anonymous')
         || ' as ' || CURRENT_ROLE;
END

curl localhost:3000/rpc/whoami -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"     # "ana@example.com as WEB_USER"
curl localhost:3000/rpc/whoami                                       # "anonymous as WEB_ANON"

The same mechanism gives you row-level security. Create a view that shows each user only their own orders:

CREATE VIEW my_orders AS
  SELECT o.* FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE c.email = RDB$GET_CONTEXT('USER_TRANSACTION', 'request.jwt.claim.sub');

GRANT SELECT ON my_orders TO ROLE web_user;

Then reload the schema cache so the new view appears:

-- in isql; other tools don't need SET TERM
SET TERM ^;
EXECUTE BLOCK AS BEGIN POST_EVENT 'fbrest_reload'; END^
SET TERM ;^
COMMIT;

curl localhost:3000/my_orders -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"     # only Ana's orders

  • Configuration: jwt-secret, jwt-aud, jwt-role-claim-key.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This tutorial runs Firebird 5 with a small bookstore database, puts FirebirdREST in front of it and walks through the main kinds of requests. You need Docker with Compose and curl.

docs.title: 1. Start everything
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/mariuz/firebirdrest
cd firebirdrest
docker compose up --build

Compose starts three containers:

Service Address What it is firebird localhost:3050 Firebird 5 with examples/bookstore.sql and bookstore-fb4.sql loaded firebirdrest http://localhost:3000 the API swagger http://localhost:8080 Swagger UI reading the API's OpenAPI document

The example has authors, books, tags (linked to books through book_tags), customers, orders and order_items, plus a view, a few procedures and functions, and two roles: web_anon can read the catalogue and web_user can do everything.

docs.title: 2. Read a table
docs.text:
curl 'localhost:3000/books'

Every table and view is an endpoint. Unquoted Firebird names are upper case in the database and lower case in the API, so BOOKS is /books and AUTHOR_ID is author_id.

Pick columns, filter and sort:

curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=title,price&price=lt.10&order=price.desc'

[{"title":"Guards! Guards!","price":9.99},{"title":"Small Gods","price":8.50},{"title":"A Wizard of Earthsea","price":7.25}]

Filters take the form column=operator.value. A few more:

curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=title&title=ilike.*god*'          # case-insensitive LIKE
curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=title&published=gte.1970&in_stock=is.true'
curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=title&or=(price.lt.8,published.lt.1965)'

See Reading tables for every operator.

docs.title: 3. Follow relationships
docs.text:
Foreign keys let you pull related rows into the same response:

curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=title,authors(name,country)&id=eq.1'

[{"title":"Guards! Guards!","authors":{"name":"Terry Pratchett","country":"UK"}}]

It works in every direction, and through junction tables:

curl 'localhost:3000/authors?select=name,books(title)&id=eq.2'      # one-to-many
curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=title,tags(name)&id=eq.1'          # many-to-many via book_tags

Add !inner to keep only rows that have a match, for example books by Polish authors:

curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=title,authors!inner(name)&authors.country=eq.Poland'

docs.title: 4. Count and summarise
docs.text:
curl 'localhost:3000/books?select=author_id,count(),total:price.sum()&order=author_id'
curl 'localhost:3000/authors?select=name,books(count)'

docs.title: 5. Call a procedure
docs.text:
Stored procedures and functions live under /rpc:

curl 'localhost:3000/rpc/books_by_country?country=UK'               # selectable procedure
curl 'localhost:3000/rpc/add_vat?amount=100'                        # function: 119.00

docs.title: 6. Try a write
docs.text:
Anonymous requests run as web_anon, which may only read:

curl -i -X POST localhost:3000/tags -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"classic"}'

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized

{"code":"28000","message":"no permission for INSERT access to TABLE TAGS","details":"Effective user is AUTHENTICATOR","hint":null}

That is Firebird refusing the INSERT, not FirebirdREST. Continue with the authentication tutorial to send requests as web_user.

docs.title: 7. Explore the API
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:8080 for Swagger UI, or fetch the OpenAPI document directly:

curl localhost:3000/

docs.title: Using your own database
docs.text:
Point FirebirdREST at any Firebird 3, 4 or 5 database:

export FBREST_DB_URI='authenticator:secret@localhost:3050/var/lib/firebird/data/app.fdb'
export FBREST_DB_ANON_ROLE=web_anon
firebirdrest

Connect as a dedicated user with no privileges of its own, and grant it the roles requests should use. Security and roles explains why and how.
